snapshots.text:
A Fenwick Tree is a Binary Indexed Tree that can be used to store frequency related data for items or intervals.

## Structure

A Fenwick Tree is a binary tree that is indexed by the bits of the key for that tree. This tree can only be implemented for keys that are integers and have a fixed range.

We typically implement Fenwick Trees using an array.

## Applications

Fenwick Trees are used to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, so the operations it supports are guided primarily by the use that it will be put to in the application above.

## Operations Supported

The Fenwick Tree supports 4 basic operations each of which take time <i>O(log2n)<i>.

### Change the frequency at some position and update the tree

### Read the Cumulative Frequency for a given key

### Read the actual(not cumulative) frequency at a certain position

### Find the index with a given cumulative frequency

It also supports a scaling operation which takes time O(n).

### Scale the entire tree by a certain factor

snapshots.text:
A Fenwick tree (also known as binary indexed tree) is a data structure that can be used to implement cumulative frequency tables. It was invented by Peter Fenwick in 1994. [1]

## Structure

A Fenwick tree is a tree that is indexed by the bits of the key for that tree. This tree can only be implemented for keys that are integers and have a fixed range.

Fenwick trees are typically implemented as arrays.

## Applications

Fenwick trees are used to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, so the operations it supports are guided primarily by the use that it will be put to in the application above.

## Supported operations

Fenwick tree supports the following basic operations each of which take O(log n) time:

Change the frequency at some position and update the tree

Read the cumulative frequency for a given key

Read the actual (not cumulative) frequency at a certain position

Find the index with a given cumulative frequency, if all individual frequencies are positive, or all indices with a given cumulative frequency, if all individual frequencies are non-negative

It also supports scaling all frequencies in the entire tree by a constant factor in O(n) time.

references.text: Peter M. Fenwick. (1994). A new data structure for cumulative frequency tables. Software: Practice and Experience. doi:10.1002/spe.4380240306

snapshots.text:
A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree is a data structure providing efficient methods for calculation and manipulation of the prefix sums of a table of values. It was proposed by Peter Fenwick in 1994.[1] Fenwick trees primarily solve the problem of balancing prefix sum calculation efficiency with the efficiency of element modification. The efficiency of these operations comes as a trade-off - greater efficiency in prefix sum calculation is achieved by pre-calculating values, but as more values are pre-calculated more must be re-calculated upon any modification to the underlying value table. Fenwick trees both calculate prefix sums and modify the table in O(log n) time, where n is the size of the table.

## Description

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers, for example). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes. Although Fenwick trees are trees in concept, in practice they are implemented using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. Given an index in the array representing a vertex, the index of a vertex's parent or child is calculated through bitwise operations on the binary representation of its index. Each index contains the pre-calculated sum of a section of the table, and by combining that sum with section sums encountered during an upward traversal to the root, the prefix sum is calculated. When a table value is modified, all section sums which contain the modified value are in turn modified during a similar traversal of the tree. The section sums are defined in such a way that queries and modifications to the table are executed in asymptotically equivalent time - O(log n) in the worst case.

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time. The sum of an arbitrary subarray can also be calculated by subtracting the prefix sum before its start index from the prefix sum at its end point.

## Applications

Fenwick trees are used to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, so the operations it supports are guided primarily by the use that it will be put to in the application above.

See also: Applications of Prefix sums

references.text: Peter M. Fenwick. (1994). A new data structure for cumulative frequency tables. Software: Practice and Experience. doi:10.1002/spe.4380240306

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree is a data structure providing efficient methods for calculation and manipulation of the prefix sums of a table of values. It was proposed by Peter Fenwick in 1994.[1] Fenwick trees primarily solve the problem of balancing prefix sum calculation efficiency with element modification efficiency. The efficiency of these operations comes as a trade-off - greater efficiency in prefix sum calculation is achieved by pre-calculating values, but as more values are pre-calculated more must be re-calculated upon any modification to the underlying value table. Fenwick trees both calculate prefix sums and modify the table in O(\log n) time, where n is the size of the table.

## Description

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers, for example). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes. Although Fenwick trees are trees in concept, in practice they are implemented using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. Given an index in the array representing a vertex, the index of a vertex's parent or child is calculated through bitwise operations on the binary representation of its index. Each index contains the pre-calculated sum of a section of the table, and by combining that sum with section sums encountered during an upward traversal to the root, the prefix sum is calculated. When a table value is modified, all section sums which contain the modified value are in turn modified during a similar traversal of the tree. The section sums are defined in such a way that queries and modifications to the table are executed in asymptotically equivalent time - O(\log n) in the worst case.

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n \log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time. The sum of an arbitrary subarray can also be calculated by subtracting the prefix sum before its start point from the prefix sum at its end point.

## Pseudocode and Example

This section will provide the pseudocode for the read and update operations to be performed.

Let the table of elements(denoted by Array[]) be empty initially.

Update Operation on an index i of the Array[] will imply adding value v in the ith position of the Array[].

Read Operation for a given index i will give the prefix sum of all the indices upto i.

Let Tree[] denote the Fenwick tree we will construct initialized to 0.

Update(i,value_to_be_added):

Tree[i]=Tree[i]+value_to_be_added

i= i + (i&(-i))

if i<= Size_Of_the_Table_Of_Elements :

Update(i,value_to_be_added)

The above Update Operation terminates in O( log n ) where n = Size Of the table of elements

Read (i) :

sum = 0

while ( i>0 ):

sum = sum + Tree[i]

i=i-(i&(-i))

return sum

Again , the above Read Operation terminates in O( log n ) where n = Size Of the table of elements

Miracles of the expression i&(-i):

Let i be denoted by a1b in binary representation , where b is a string of 0's. Then -i will denote a_c1b . Now if we do Logical conjunction of both i and -i , we will get a0b .

Subtracting (i&(-i)) from i will give us the value of 1b

Example :

Let Array[] = [0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]

Query 1: Update 4 by adding 10 .

Array[] = [ 0, 0, 0,10, 0, 0, 0, 0]

Tree[] = [ 0, 0, 0,10, 0, 0, 0,10]

Query 2:: Update 2 by adding 13

Array[] = [ 0,13, 0,10, 0, 0, 0, 0]

Tree[] = [ 0,13, 0,23, 0, 0, 0,23]

Query 3:: Return prefix sum for index 5

Read function will iterate through index 5 and 4 of the Tree[] to get the answer.

Query 4:: Update 5 by adding 17

Array[] = [ 0,13, 0,10,17, 0, 0, 0]

Tree[] = [ 0,13, 0,23,17,17, 0,40]

Query 5:: Return prefix sum for index 8

Read Function will only read the 8th index of the Tree[] to get the answer.

## Applications

Fenwick trees are used to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it is very easy to generate the cumulative sum table. From this cumulative sum table it is possible to calculate the summation of the frequencies in a certain range in order of O(\log n) .

Fenwick tree can also be used to update and query ranges in multidimensional arrays with complexity O(2^d* \log ^d n) , where d is number of dimensions and n is the number of elements along each dimension. [2]

references.text: Peter M. Fenwick. (1994). A new data structure for cumulative frequency tables. Software: Practice and Experience. doi:10.1002/spe.4380240306
Pushkar Mishra. (2013). On Updating and Querying Sub-arrays of Multidimensional Arrays. http://arxiv.org/abs/1311.6093

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers. This structure was proposed by Peter Fenwick in 1994 to improve the efficiency of arithmetic coding compression algorithms.[1]

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves much higher performance for two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. In a flat array of n numbers, calculating prefix sum and udating the elements both require O(n) time. Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree, where the value of each node is the sum of the numbers in that subtree. The tree structure allows operations to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Description

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers, for example). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes. Although Fenwick trees are trees in concept, in practice they are implemented using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. Given an index in the array representing a vertex, the index of a vertex's parent or child is calculated through bitwise operations on the binary representation of its index. Each index contains the pre-calculated sum of a section of the table, and by combining that sum with section sums encountered during an upward traversal to the root, the prefix sum is calculated. When a table value is modified, all section sums which contain the modified value are in turn modified during a similar traversal of the tree. The section sums are defined in such a way that queries and modifications to the table are executed in asymptotically equivalent time - O(\log n) in the worst case.

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n \log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time. The sum of an arbitrary subarray can also be calculated by subtracting the prefix sum before its start point from the prefix sum at its end point.

## Applications

Fenwick trees are used to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree is very easy to generate the cumulative sum table. From this cumulative sum table it is possible to calculate the summation of the frequencies in a certain range in order of O(\log n) .

Fenwick trees can also be used to update and query subarrays of multidimensional arrays. These operations can be performed with complexity O(2^d \log ^d n) , where d is number of dimensions and n is the number of elements along each dimension.[2]

## Implementation

A simple C implementation follows.

Pushkar Mishra. (2013). A New Algorithm for Updating and Querying Sub-arrays of Multidimensional Arrays.

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree, where the value of each node is the sum of the numbers in that subtree. The tree structure allows operations to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero).

Fenwick trees can be extended to update and query subarrays of multidimensional arrays. These operations can be performed with complexity O(2^d \log ^d n) , where d is number of dimensions and n is the number of elements along each dimension.[2]

## Description

Although Fenwick trees are trees in concept, in practice they are implemented as an [[implicit data structure] using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. Given an index in the array representing a vertex, the index of a vertex's parent or child is calculated through bitwise operations on the binary representation of its index. Each element of the array contains the pre-calculated sum of a range of values, and by combining that sum with additional ranges encountered during an upward traversal to the root, the prefix sum is calculated. When a table value is modified, all range sums which contain the modified value are in turn modified during a similar traversal of the tree. The range sums are defined in such a way that both queries and modifications to the table are executed in asymptotically equivalent time ( O(\log n) in the worst case).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array. Each element i whose index is a power of 2 contains the sum of the first i elements. Elements whose indices are the sum of two (distinct) powers of 2 contain the sum of the the elements since the preceding power of 2. In general, each element contains the sum of the values since its parent in the tree, and that parent is found by clearing the least-significant bit in the index.

To find the sum up to any given index, consider the binary expansion of the index, and add elements which correspond to each 1 bit in the binary form.

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1 bits, so three elements must be added: 10002, 10102, and 10112. These contain the sums of values 1–8, 9–10, and 11, respectively.

To modify the eleventh value, the elements which must be modified are 10112, 11002, 100002, and all higher powers of 2 up to the size of the array. These contain the sums of values 11, 9–12, and 1–16, respectively. The maximum number of elements which may need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array.

## Implementation

A simple C implementation follows. The setup phase takes about five times longer than for a simple flat array, but the subsequent queries are (because of the large array used) about 1600 times faster.

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers.

This structure was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989[1]

with a further modification published in 1992.[2]

It has subsequently become known under the name Fenwick tree after Peter Fenwick, who described this structure in his 1994 article.[3]

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. A flat array of n numbers can either store the elements or the prefix sums. In the first case, computing prefix sums requires linear time; in the second case, updating the array elements requires linear time (in both cases, the other operation can be performed in constant time). Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree, where the value of each node is the sum of the numbers in that subtree. The tree structure allows operations to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero).

Fenwick trees can be extended to update and query subarrays of multidimensional arrays. These operations can be performed with complexity O(4^d \log^d n) , where d is number of dimensions and n is the number of elements along each dimension.[4]

## Description

Although Fenwick trees are trees in concept, in practice they are implemented as an implicit data structure using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. Given an index in the array representing a vertex, the index of a vertex's parent or child is calculated through bitwise operations on the binary representation of its index. Each element of the array contains the pre-calculated sum of a range of values, and by combining that sum with additional ranges encountered during an upward traversal to the root, the prefix sum is calculated. When a table value is modified, all range sums that contain the modified value are in turn modified during a similar traversal of the tree. The range sums are defined such that both queries and modifications to the table are executed in asymptotically equivalent time ( O(\log n) in the worst case).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array. Each element whose index i is a power of 2 contains the sum of the first i elements. Elements whose indices are the sum of two (distinct) powers of 2 contain the sum of the elements since the preceding power of 2. In general, each element contains the sum of the values since its parent in the tree, and that parent is found by clearing the least significant bit in the index.

To find the sum up to any given index, consider the binary expansion of the index and add elements corresponding to each 1 bit in the binary form.

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1 bits, so three elements must be added: 10002, 10102, and 10112. These contain the sums of values 1–8, 9–10, and 11, respectively.

To modify the eleventh value, the elements that must be modified are 10112, 11002, 100002, and all higher powers of 2 up to the size of the array. These contain the sums of values 11, 9–12, and 1–16, respectively. The maximum number of elements that may need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array.

Compute i' = ( i rounded up to nearest multiple of 2^j )

This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree with n+1 nodes where the value of each node in the tree is the prefix sum of the array from the index of the parent (inclusive) up to the index of the node (exclusive). The tree itself is implicit and can be stored as an array of n numbers, with the implicit root node omitted from the array. The tree structure allows the operations of element retrieval, element update, prefix sum, and range sum to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero). It is also possible to construct extensions of this data structure to quickly compute cumulative sums on d -dimensional arrays in O(\log^d n) time.[4]

## Description

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array A[n] with n elements. The corresponding Fenwick tree has n+1 nodes with an implicit node 0 at the root. Each level k of the tree contains nodes with indices corresponding to sums of k distinct powers of 2 (with k=0 representing an empty sum 0). For example, level k=1 contains nodes 1=2^0, 2=2^1, 4=2^2, ... and level k=2 contains nodes 3=2^1 + 2^0, 5 = 2^2 + 2^0, 6 = 2^2 + 2^1, ... The parent of a given node can be found by clearing the last set bit (LSB) in its index, corresponding to the smallest power of 2 in its sum. For example, the parent of 6 = 1102 is 4 = 1002 .

The below diagram shows the structure of a 16-node Fenwick tree, corresponding to a 15-element array A:

Let A(i,j] = \{ A[k] \}_{k=i+1}^j . The value of a node at index i corresponds to the range sum of elements in A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] , that is, the values of A starting after the parent's index up to the current node's index, inclusive. The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node[3] and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. Note that the indices in this range do not directly correspond to children of i : for example, the range of responsibility for node 2 is A(0,2] = \{A[1], A[2]\} but node 1 is not a child of node 2. The root node 0 contains the sum of the empty range A(0,0] = \{\} with value 0.

Typically, the Fenwick tree is implemented as an implicit data structure using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. In this representation, the root node 0 is omitted and the array indices directly correspond to node indices in the tree (using 1-based indexing).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

### Range query

To find the prefix sum up to any given index (the "range query" operation), add up the values of nodes along the path from the current index to the root of the tree (which is trivially an empty sum, 0). The number of values to add (excluding the implicit root) is equal to the number of 1-bits in the index, and is at most \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , giving a time complexity of O(\log n) .

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1-bits, so three node values must be added: those at nodes 11=10112, 10=10102, and 8=10002 (the implicit root node of 00002 can be ignored). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,10], and A[1,8], respectively (where A[i,j] = {A[i], A[i+1], ..., A[j]}) .

### Point update

To update the value in a Fenwick tree at index i (corresponding to assigning A[i] a new value) (the "point update" operation):

Compute the delta \delta = A[i]_\mathrm{new} - A[i]_\mathrm{old} .

Then, while index i \leq n :

Update the index by adding LSB: i \leftarrow i + (i\ \&\ (-i))

Add \delta to the value at node i .

Intuitively, this can be thought of as updating each node (starting with i and iterating in increasing order) whose range of responsibility includes A[i] .

For example, updating value 11=10112 in a 16-element array requires updating 10112, (10112 + 12 = 11002), and (11002 + 1002 = 100002). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,12], and A[1,16], respectively. Again, the maximum number of nodes that need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array, \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , and the time complexity is thus O(\log n) .

### Building the tree

A naive way to construct the tree would be to initialize the tree values to 0 and perform n point updates, yielding a time complexity of O(n\log n) . However, an alternate approach uses dynamic programming to build the tree up incrementally along increasing indices. Initialization proceeds as follows:

Copy array A[n] into array T[n] containing tree values

For each index i from 1 to n:

Let j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) . This is the first node larger than i that contains A[i] in its range of responsibility.

If j \leq n , update value of node at j: T[j] \leftarrow T[j] + T[i]

It can be shown that at the point that index i is reached in the loop, T[i] is already the correct Fenwick value for node i . If i is a leaf node (with only one element in its range of responsibility) this holds trivially. If i is an internal node, the loop ensures that it has been updated with all range sums within its own range, so it will contain the correct Fenwick value. For example, at step i=4 , node 4 (with initial value A[4] ) will have been incremented by T[2] (which contains the sum A[1] + A[2] ) and T[3] (which contains the value A[3] ), and thus will contain the range sum A(0,4] of the first 4 elements of the tree.

Since each update happens at most once per index, the resulting algorithm is O(n) time complexity. This can also be done in-place in the original array, eliminating the copy and additional storage for T[n] .

An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n] , by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep.

A less efficient O(n) algorithm for constructing the tree works in two passes: first convert A[n] to a prefix sum (which takes O(n) time), then iterating backwards from n..1, compute each node's range sum by computing the difference of prefix sums: \Sigma A(\mathrm{parent}(i), i] = \Sigma A(0, i] - \Sigma A(0, \mathrm{parent}(i)] .[5]

### Extension to multiple dimensions

A 2D Fenwick tree (2D BIT) can be constructed as a 1D Fenwick tree where each node of the tree contains a 1D Fenwick tree,[4] and stores range sums for submatrices of a 2D matrix A[m,n]. The tree representation remains implicit and the data is stored in an m x n array where position (i, j) in the array corresponds to the jth node of the ith Fenwick tree.

Point update and range query are implemented similarly to the 1D case, but using nested loops (iterating along the column dimension (sub-tree) in the inner loop, and iterating along the row dimension (main tree) in the outer loop).

This idea can be extended to tensors with arbitrary number of dimensions d, with time complexity O(\log^d n) for range-query and point-update (assuming the tensor is size n along each axis).

## Applications

### Keeping track of positions problem

Assume one have a set of elements, with an integer displacement. Then Array[i] would store relative displacement to previous element, where i is an element number.

By taking range sum between i and j, one would get the relative distance between object i and j.

A concrete real example of this would be tags in html file, where one keep track of line numbers of every element when a element is moved.

To get a position, one simply take the range sum between two elements.

### Vehicle tracking problem

Given N regions and a maximum of 64 types of vehicles, how to find a vehicle of spesific type (taxi, bus, train) in fastet possible way

By associating a bit position to a correspodning vehicle, in an integer, one can keep track of all types of vehicles in a spesific region.

By using XOR operation, which do have an inverse, one can find location if a vehicle is in set of regions by taking a range XOR between

to postitions i,j in fenwick tree.

By taking binary search of fenwick tree, with taking lower index equal to position one are standing at, one can get a vehicle of spesific type nearby a spesific location.

An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n] , by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep.

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree (BIT) is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers.

This structure was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989[1]

with a further modification published in 1992.[2]

It has subsequently become known under the name Fenwick tree after Peter Fenwick, who described this structure in his 1994 article.[3]

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. A flat array of n numbers can either store the elements or the prefix sums. In the first case, computing prefix sums requires linear time; in the second case, updating the array elements requires linear time (in both cases, the other operation can be performed in constant time). Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree with n+1 nodes where the value of each node in the tree is the prefix sum of the array from the index of the parent (inclusive) up to the index of the node (exclusive). The tree itself is implicit and can be stored as an array of n numbers, with the implicit root node omitted from the array. The tree structure allows the operations of element retrieval, element update, prefix sum, and range sum to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero). It is also possible to construct extensions of this data structure to quickly compute cumulative sums on d -dimensional arrays in O(\log^d n) time.[4]

## Description

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array A[n] with n elements. The corresponding Fenwick tree has n+1 nodes with an implicit node 0 at the root. Each level k of the tree contains nodes with indices corresponding to sums of k distinct powers of 2 (with k=0 representing an empty sum 0). For example, level k=1 contains nodes 1=2^0, 2=2^1, 4=2^2, ... and level k=2 contains nodes 3=2^1 + 2^0, 5 = 2^2 + 2^0, 6 = 2^2 + 2^1, ... The parent of a given node can be found by clearing the last set bit (LSB) in its index, corresponding to the smallest power of 2 in its sum. For example, the parent of 6 = 1102 is 4 = 1002 .

The below diagram shows the structure of a 16-node Fenwick tree, corresponding to a 15-element array A:

Let A(i,j] = \{ A[k] \}_{k=i+1}^j . The value of a node at index i corresponds to the range sum of elements in A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] , that is, the values of A starting after the parent's index up to the current node's index, inclusive. The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node[3] and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. Note that the indices in this range do not directly correspond to children of i : for example, the range of responsibility for node 2 is A(0,2] = \{A[1], A[2]\} but node 1 is not a child of node 2. The root node 0 contains the sum of the empty range A(0,0] = \{\} with value 0.

Typically, the Fenwick tree is implemented as an implicit data structure using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. In this representation, the root node 0 is omitted and the array indices directly correspond to node indices in the tree (using 1-based indexing).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

### Range query

To find the prefix sum up to any given index (the "range query" operation), add up the values of nodes along the path from the current index to the root of the tree (which is trivially an empty sum, 0). The number of values to add (excluding the implicit root) is equal to the number of 1-bits in the index, and is at most \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , giving a time complexity of O(\log n) .

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1-bits, so three node values must be added: those at nodes 11=10112, 10=10102, and 8=10002 (the implicit root node of 00002 can be ignored). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,10], and A[1,8], respectively (where A[i,j] = {A[i], A[i+1], ..., A[j]}) .

### Point update

To update the value in a Fenwick tree at index i (corresponding to assigning A[i] a new value) (the "point update" operation):

Compute the delta \delta = A[i]_\mathrm{new} - A[i]_\mathrm{old} .

Then, while index i \leq n :

Update the index by adding LSB: i \leftarrow i + (i\ \&\ (-i))

Add \delta to the value at node i .

Intuitively, this can be thought of as updating each node (starting with i and iterating in increasing order) whose range of responsibility includes A[i] .

For example, updating value 11=10112 in a 16-element array requires updating 10112, (10112 + 12 = 11002), and (11002 + 1002 = 100002). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,12], and A[1,16], respectively. Again, the maximum number of nodes that need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array, \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , and the time complexity is thus O(\log n) .

### Building the tree

A naive way to construct the tree would be to initialize the tree values to 0 and perform n point updates, yielding a time complexity of O(n\log n) . However, an alternate approach uses dynamic programming to build the tree up incrementally along increasing indices. Initialization proceeds as follows:

Copy array A[n] into array T[n] containing tree values

For each index i from 1 to n:

Let j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) . This is the first node larger than i that contains A[i] in its range of responsibility.

If j \leq n , update value of node at j: T[j] \leftarrow T[j] + T[i]

It can be shown that at the point that index i is reached in the loop, T[i] is already the correct Fenwick value for node i . If i is a leaf node (with only one element in its range of responsibility) this holds trivially. If i is an internal node, the loop ensures that it has been updated with all range sums within its own range, so it will contain the correct Fenwick value. For example, at step i=4 , node 4 (with initial value A[4] ) will have been incremented by T[2] (which contains the sum A[1] + A[2] ) and T[3] (which contains the value A[3] ), and thus will contain the range sum A(0,4] of the first 4 elements of the tree.

Since each update happens at most once per index, the resulting algorithm is O(n) time complexity. This can also be done in-place in the original array, eliminating the copy and additional storage for T[n] .

An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n] , by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep.

A less efficient O(n) algorithm for constructing the tree works in two passes: first convert A[n] to a prefix sum (which takes O(n) time), then iterating backwards from n..1, compute each node's range sum by computing the difference of prefix sums: \Sigma A(\mathrm{parent}(i), i] = \Sigma A(0, i] - \Sigma A(0, \mathrm{parent}(i)] .[5]

A 2D Fenwick tree (2D BIT) can be constructed as a 1D Fenwick tree where each node of the tree contains a 1D Fenwick tree,[4] and stores range sums for submatrices of a 2D matrix A[m,n]. The tree representation remains implicit and the data is stored in an m x n array where position (i, j) in the array corresponds to the jth node of the ith Fenwick tree.

Point update and range query are implemented similarly to the 1D case, but using nested loops (iterating along the column dimension (sub-tree) in the inner loop, and iterating along the row dimension (main tree) in the outer loop).

This idea can be extended to tensors with arbitrary number of dimensions d, with time complexity O(\log^d n) for range-query and point-update (assuming the tensor is size n along each axis).

The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node[3] and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. Note that the indices in this range do not directly correspond to children of i : for example, the range of responsibility for node 2 is A(0,2] = \{A[1], A[2]\} but node 1 is not a child of node 2. The root node 0 contains the sum of the empty range A(0,0] = \{\} with value 0.

Typically, the Fenwick tree is implemented as an implicit data structure using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. In this representation, the root node 0 is omitted and the array indices directly correspond to node indices in the tree (using 1-based indexing).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

### Range query

To find the prefix sum up to any given index (the "range query" operation), add up the values of nodes along the path from the current index to the root of the tree (which is trivially an empty sum, 0). The number of values to add (excluding the implicit root) is equal to the number of 1-bits in the index, and is at most \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , giving a time complexity of O(\log n) .

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1-bits, so three node values must be added: those at nodes 11=10112, 10=10102, and 8=10002 (the implicit root node of 00002 can be ignored). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,10], and A[1,8], respectively (where A[i,j] = {A[i], A[i+1], ..., A[j]}) .

### Point update

To update the value in a Fenwick tree at index i (corresponding to assigning A[i] a new value) (the "point update" operation):

Compute the delta \delta = A[i]_\mathrm{new} - A[i]_\mathrm{old} .

Then, while index i \leq n :

Update the index by adding LSB: i \leftarrow i + (i\ \&\ (-i))

Add \delta to the value at node i .

Intuitively, this can be thought of as updating each node (starting with i and iterating in increasing order) whose range of responsibility includes A[i] .

For example, updating value 11=10112 in a 16-element array requires updating 10112, (10112 + 12 = 11002), and (11002 + 1002 = 100002). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,12], and A[1,16], respectively. Again, the maximum number of nodes that need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array, \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , and the time complexity is thus O(\log n) .

### Building the tree

A naive way to construct the tree would be to initialize the tree values to 0 and perform n point updates, yielding a time complexity of O(n\log n) . However, an alternate approach uses dynamic programming to build the tree up incrementally along increasing indices. Initialization proceeds as follows:

Copy array A[n] into array T[n] containing tree values

For each index i from 1 to n:

Let j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) . This is the first node larger than i that contains A[i] in its range of responsibility.

If j \leq n , update value of node at j: T[j] \leftarrow T[j] + T[i]

It can be shown that at the point that index i is reached in the loop, T[i] is already the correct Fenwick value for node i . If i is a leaf node (with only one element in its range of responsibility) this holds trivially. If i is an internal node, the loop ensures that it has been updated with all range sums within its own range, so it will contain the correct Fenwick value. For example, at step i=4 , node 4 (with initial value A[4] ) will have been incremented by T[2] (which contains the sum A[1] + A[2] ) and T[3] (which contains the value A[3] ), and thus will contain the range sum A(0,4] of the first 4 elements of the tree.

Since each update happens at most once per index, the resulting algorithm is O(n) time complexity. This can also be done in-place in the original array, eliminating the copy and additional storage for T[n] .

An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n] , by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep.

A less efficient O(n) algorithm for constructing the tree works in two passes: first convert A[n] to a prefix sum (which takes O(n) time), then iterating backwards from n..1, compute each node's range sum by computing the difference of prefix sums: \Sigma A(\mathrm{parent}(i), i] = \Sigma A(0, i] - \Sigma A(0, \mathrm{parent}(i)] .[5]

### Extension to multiple dimensions

A 2D Fenwick tree (2D BIT) can be constructed as a 1D Fenwick tree where each node of the tree contains a 1D Fenwick tree,[4] and stores range sums for submatrices of a 2D matrix A[m,n]. The tree representation remains implicit and the data is stored in an m x n array where position (i, j) in the array corresponds to the jth node of the ith Fenwick tree.

Point update and range query are implemented similarly to the 1D case, but using nested loops (iterating along the column dimension (sub-tree) in the inner loop, and iterating along the row dimension (main tree) in the outer loop).

This idea can be extended to tensors with arbitrary number of dimensions d, with time complexity O(\log^d n) for range-query and point-update (assuming the tensor is size n along each axis).

## Applications

### Keeping track of positions problem

Assume one have a set of elements, with an integer displacement. Then Array[i] would store relative displacement to previous element, where i is an element number.

By taking range sum between i and j, one would get the relative distance between object i and j.

A concrete real example of this would be tags in html file, where one keep track of line numbers of every element when an element is moved.

To get a position, one simply take the range sum between two elements.

### Find range of angle for a ray to hit N mirrors, when last mirror is given

Assume one have N mirrors

Objective is to find an angle theta, that adjust a light ray (from a light source) such that it hits all 2D mirrors by reflection. Reverse the problem, and try instead to find range of incoming theta for mirror to hit a spesific mirror.

That is:

Mirror 1: Range 1 -> Mirror 2, Range 3 -> Mirror 5

Mirror 2: Range 1 -> Mirror 6

...etc

For each pair, convert needed outgoing range to needed incoming range.

Assume there is a spesific end mirror.

Main idea here is to roll the ball of overlap of incoming and outgoing ranges, down in the tree of mirrors.

Incoming range for each mirror will become larger and larger, and in the end light source ray just need to see what mirror that can be hit within incoming range.

One can use fenwick tree for each mirror, that remembers allowed incoming ranges.

By doing this, one can in a fast way update allowed ranges when need.

Lets say end mirror is 5. If mirror 2, mirror 8 -> mirror 5, then mirror 2 and mirror 8 needs an update of allowed ranges. Allowed range will be the overlap.

All neighbours is updated, and have its allowed incoming updated by setting range to 1. Because on can go both mirror 2 -> mirror 8 -> miror 5 and mirror 2 -> mirror 5,

one may have two ranges of 1 inside mirror 2. One have updated mirror 2 -> mirror 5 and mirror 8 -> mirror 5, but by looking at mirror 2 -> mirror 8 one can add

another range to incoming range of mirror 2. We have 3 nodes now. When adding new node, one must update all incoming for all nodes against new node.

Continue doing this until all mirrors are added.

When all is added, try to see what mirror that can be hit, and with what range, from light source.

Remember all ranges, and add occurence by 1 for theta in range in fenwick tree. Fenwick tree must be very large, to handle very small theta. Use numerical compression to handle this, that is 0.00001 -> 0, 0.00002 -> 1, 0.00003 -> 2...etc

### Sub-range product of transformation matrices

Create two fenwick trees, one with product over inverses and one with product of its usal matrices.

To find sub-range product, take product range of matrices in inverse fenwick tree to left side of range.

Remember this matrix.

Now, take product range of matrices in fenwick tree to right side of range.

Take product of this matrix with the inverse matrix one got from inverse fenwick tree.

By doing this, one can update a matrix, without doing all the recalculations. Important thing here, is to update both matrix and its inverse

### Longest increasing subsequence

Consider a sequence

For each element v added, update A[i] s.t:

A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1, such that array[x] <= array[i].

array[x] <= array[i] can be ensured, by letting i= array[index in list].

This leaves ous with:

A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1,

A running example:

A[array[0]] = A[8] = max (0 <= x < 8) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[1]] = A[5] = max (0 <= x < 5) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[2]] = A[7] = max (0 <= x < 7) A[x]+ 1 = max(A[0],[1],A[2],A[3],A[4],A[5],A[6]) + 1 = A[5] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2

A[array[3]] = A[3] = max (0 <= x < 3) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[4]] = A[1] = max (0 <= x < 1) A[x] + 1 = max(A[0]) + 1 = 1

A[array[5]] = A[2] = max (0 <= x < 2) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1) + 1 = 2

A[array[6]] = A[9] = max (0 <= x < 9) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,0,1,0,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3

A[array[7]] = A[4] = max (0 <= x < 4) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3

A[array[8]] = A[6] = max (0 <= x < 6) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,3,1) + 1 = 3+1 = 4

That corresponds well to the answer 1,2,4,6

If max element is to large, one can use number compression by using sorting

That is i= indexInSortedList[index in not sorted list], instead of i = array[index in not sorted list]

Take this example:

Array: 166,32,44,66,88

Sorted: 32,44,66,88,166

Then:

A[indexInSortedList[0]] = A[4], and we are back to the problem we are used to

### Find range with smallest sum that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One has a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurrence is remembered,

removing elements from left side won't do any damage.

One can check if an element is already found, by checking it against an array of indexes of last occurrence for this number. Furthermore, one can check if index one is standing on, is last occurrence by comparing with index in array.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find range with smallest sum that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Find smallest range that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One have a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurence is remembered,

removing elements from left side wont do any damage.

By setting values of last occurence of element in set S to 1, value not in set S to 0, and elment in S that is not last occurence to 0, one

can use fenwick tree combined with range sum to find smallest range that contains all elements in set S.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find smallest range that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Use of fenwick in k-mean algorithm, to make mean calculation faster

Create a sepreate fenwick tree for x and y coordinate.

Allocate empty space for coordinates to a variable N (max number of coordinates for each component) for each M components. Each of the empty spaces has value 0.

Create a list of initial means, and allocate coordinates to nearest mean (update empty allocated space, corresponding to component associated with mean, in fenwick tree).

Remember to keep track of number of coordinates in each component.

After this is done, find sum of each component and divide by number of coordinates in corresponding component.

Then swap each coordinate between components if needed, by substracting and adding values.

Remember to update number of coordinates in each components

Notice, that comparing to mean step is still O(n). The swap is slower; O(log n) compared to O(1). Mean calculation is faster; O(Mlog N), where M is number of components, compared to O(N).

### Flow calculations, where each components has max 8 neighbours

Create a 2D grid, where one keep track of input flow (negative value) and output flow (positive value) in following way:

Out 0 Out 0 Out

0 In In In 0

Out In 0 In Out

0 In In In 0

Out 0 Out 0 Out

By placing adjacent components next to eachother, one can create a gigantic map where one keep track of flows between components.

Here on can use 2D fenwick to sum flow across a set of components, that corresponds to a path.

In some cases, in for examples pipe systems, number of components may be many thousands.

By placing all those thousand components (for example pipes) next to eachother, one can easily calculate netto flow in a very fast way, at the same time

one can update input and output flow for each component in a fast way.

In some cases, one may have to do multiple calculations and then sum total flow of all calculations - because one only can sum in one direction at a time, due to direction change.

It could also be a crowd sensing system, where one receive GPS coordinates that is associated with a square in a map.

By updating input and output based on square one leaved and square one entered, one can have a gigantic map of many thousands squares where

netto flow can be calculated in a fast way.

### Data aggregation in fog computing

Assume one have 1000 clients A1-A1000 , a fog computer B, and a server C.

By using B as a middle man, one can create a summary of statistic that is relevant to C; based on relevant actions (max,min,product, sum) and ranges.

Communication beteen A1-A1000 and B:

A sends (index, value, datatype, action (add/sub/prod/max/min)) to B.

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Update array[index] with corresponding action and value.

Communication between B and C:

B asks for a summary of statistics in format (index range, action, return data type).

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Use fenwick range operation corresponding to index range and action, and convert to desired data type.

### Keep track of locations of cars in a large map

By letting a bit position in a number correspond to a car, one can decide that 1 means that the car is here and 0 means it doesn't.

By adding and substracting a number where it is 1 in this position and 0 in the rest, one can add and remove a car from a location.

A map can be thought of as a grid, and therfore one can use 2D fenwick tree.

Because a number only have a maximum of 64 bits, one need a new fenwick tree for each chunk of 64 cars.

Each car is tagged with (fenwickTreeNr, bitPos), and each location is tagged with an index.

If a client knows its (fenwickTreeNr,bitPos) and know what location corresponds to what index, one can just update locally

and send the index instead of the GPS coordinate.

By doing this, the server does not really know where the car is - but it can search for it in a fast way by combinding binary search (adjust right side first, and then left) and range sum query. Its

also a more secure way of dealing with locations, compared to GPS coordinates.

### Fast Sub range integration, where values are time dependent

Recall simpsons formula:

\begin{align}

\int_a^b f(x)\, dx

&\approx \frac{1}{3} h\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2}\big[f(x_{2i - 2}) + 4f(x_{2i - 1}) + f(x_{2i})\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\big[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \dots + 2f(x_{n - 2}) + 4f(x_{n - 1}) + f(x_n)\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\left[f(x_0) + 4\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2} f(x_{2i - 1}) + 2\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2 - 1} f(x_{2i}) + f(x_n)\right].

\end{align}

By adding and substracting

\begin{align}f(x_{index}), 2f(x_{index})\end{align} , or

\begin{align}

4f(x_{index})

\end{align} , depending on index, to

array[index]; one can in a fast way recalculate the integral of sub ranges, when some values changes.

Notice that one can add new values by changing value of array[max index] and array[max index - 1] , and by adding new value to array[max index+1].

### Grid surface, and collions with small objects

A grid surface contains many squares or faces. By making a 2D fenwick tree, one can keep track of current preasure

each square.

By having a rule engine, that says:

Area >= 1000, must have p < 0.5. action if fail: rotation of relevant squares

Area >= 100, must have p <= 0.1, action if fail: animation played for relevant squares

Area >= 10, must have p <= 0.001 action if fail: translation of relevant suqares

One can check different ranges, in a fast way, to see if preasure constraint is OK.

If a constraint fail, an associated action can be used (f.ex a geometric transformation based on presure, and other parameters).

When first rule is checked for all possible ranges, one check next rule to see if a preasure constraint fail - if it does, a smaller area can be

affected by an predefined action.

Because a 2D fenwick tree is used, its possible to add and remove collisions to the grid. Such collisions could be bullets that hit a person in a 3D game, where a person

has surface grid (to simply one could have a rectangular surface grid). Rule engines controlls wether or not, one looses a finger, an arm, a head,..etc, based

on preasure distrubition). In some cases, a object may have life time - it may be removed after a fixed amount of time, or change in preasure as a function of time.

Its also handy to use 2D fenwick tree, when preasure waves is introduced (waves in water, earth quacke, explosions). Wave equations is used to predict grid squares affected, and these squares is updated accordanly. For each step (everyone is updated by a time step), one take a look on rule engine to see if some actions is triggered.

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree (BIT) is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers.

This structure was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989[1]

with a further modification published in 1992.[2]

It has subsequently become known under the name Fenwick tree after Peter Fenwick, who described this structure in his 1994 article.[3]

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. A flat array of n numbers can either store the elements or the prefix sums. In the first case, computing prefix sums requires linear time; in the second case, updating the array elements requires linear time (in both cases, the other operation can be performed in constant time). Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree with n+1 nodes where the value of each node in the tree is the prefix sum of the array from the index of the parent (inclusive) up to the index of the node (exclusive). The tree itself is implicit and can be stored as an array of n numbers, with the implicit root node omitted from the array. The tree structure allows the operations of element retrieval, element update, prefix sum, and range sum to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero). It is also possible to construct extensions of this data structure to quickly compute cumulative sums on d -dimensional arrays in O(\log^d n) time.[4]

## Description

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array A[n] with n elements. The corresponding Fenwick tree has n+1 nodes with an implicit node 0 at the root. Each level k of the tree contains nodes with indices corresponding to sums of k distinct powers of 2 (with k=0 representing an empty sum 0). For example, level k=1 contains nodes 1=2^0, 2=2^1, 4=2^2, ... and level k=2 contains nodes 3=2^1 + 2^0, 5 = 2^2 + 2^0, 6 = 2^2 + 2^1, ... The parent of a given node can be found by clearing the last set bit (LSB) in its index, corresponding to the smallest power of 2 in its sum. For example, the parent of 6 = 1102 is 4 = 1002 .

The below diagram shows the structure of a 16-node Fenwick tree, corresponding to a 15-element array A:

Let A(i,j] = \{ A[k] \}_{k=i+1}^j . The value of a node at index i corresponds to the range sum of elements in A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] , that is, the values of A starting after the parent's index up to the current node's index, inclusive. The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node[3] and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. ### Fenwick tree as a compression of a binary tree

A binary tree can be compressed to a fenwick tree, if and only if, for every even leaf node in binary tree (indexed 2n, n is integer ),

it is has the same property as its parents, up to the point; the smallest sub-tree that is possible to make,connecting as many nodes as possible, is created

To decompress, just do the opposit as done in compression

Subtrees may also be compressed to fenwick tree.

Furthermore, if only small changes is needed to make an fenwick compression, one should remember and do necessery changes - with the changes as extra information, to enable decompression.

### Generate fenwick compressable binary tree from its leafs

A fenwick compressable binary tree can be generated from its leaf nodes, if all leaf nodes with index k2^i is connected to node with index 2^i(k+1)

in such a way node with index 2^i(k+1) is parent of node with index k2^i.

### Keeping track of positions problem

Assume one have a set of elements, with an integer displacement. Then Array[i] would store relative displacement to previous element, where i is an element number.

By taking range sum between i and j, one would get the relative distance between object i and j.

A concrete real example of this would be tags in html file, where one keep track of line numbers of every element when an element is moved.

To get a position, one simply take the range sum between two elements.

### Sub-range product of transformation matrices

Create two fenwick trees, one with product over inverses and one with product of its usal matrices.

To find sub-range product, take product range of matrices in inverse fenwick tree to left side of range.

Remember this matrix.

Now, take product range of matrices in fenwick tree to right side of range.

Take product of this matrix with the inverse matrix one got from inverse fenwick tree.

By doing this, one can update a matrix, without doing all the recalculations. Important thing here, is to update both matrix and its inverse

### Longest increasing subsequence

Consider a sequence

For each element v added, update A[i] s.t:

A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1, such that array[x] <= array[i].

array[x] <= array[i] can be ensured, by letting i= array[index in list].

This leaves ous with:

A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1,

A running example:

A[array[0]] = A[8] = max (0 <= x < 8) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[1]] = A[5] = max (0 <= x < 5) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[2]] = A[7] = max (0 <= x < 7) A[x]+ 1 = max(A[0],[1],A[2],A[3],A[4],A[5],A[6]) + 1 = A[5] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2

A[array[3]] = A[3] = max (0 <= x < 3) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0...,0) + 1 = 1

A[array[4]] = A[1] = max (0 <= x < 1) A[x] + 1 = max(A[0]) + 1 = 1

A[array[5]] = A[2] = max (0 <= x < 2) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1) + 1 = 2

A[array[6]] = A[9] = max (0 <= x < 9) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,0,1,0,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3

A[array[7]] = A[4] = max (0 <= x < 4) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3

A[array[8]] = A[6] = max (0 <= x < 6) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,3,1) + 1 = 3+1 = 4

That corresponds well to the answer 1,2,4,6

If max element is to large, one can use number compression by using sorting

That is i= indexInSortedList[index in not sorted list], instead of i = array[index in not sorted list]

Take this example:

Array: 166,32,44,66,88

Sorted: 32,44,66,88,166

Then:

A[indexInSortedList[0]] = A[4], and we are back to the problem we are used to

### Find range with smallest sum that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One has a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurrence is remembered,

removing elements from left side won't do any damage.

One can check if an element is already found, by checking it against an array of indexes of last occurrence for this number. Furthermore, one can check if index one is standing on, is last occurrence by comparing with index in array.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find range with smallest sum that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Find smallest range that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One have a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurence is remembered,

removing elements from left side wont do any damage.

By setting values of last occurence of element in set S to 1, value not in set S to 0, and elment in S that is not last occurence to 0, one

can use fenwick tree combined with range sum to find smallest range that contains all elements in set S.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find smallest range that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Use of fenwick in k-mean algorithm, to make mean calculation faster

Create a sepreate fenwick tree for x and y coordinate.

Allocate empty space for coordinates to a variable N (max number of coordinates for each component) for each M components. Each of the empty spaces has value 0.

Create a list of initial means, and allocate coordinates to nearest mean (update empty allocated space, corresponding to component associated with mean, in fenwick tree).

Remember to keep track of number of coordinates in each component.

After this is done, find sum of each component and divide by number of coordinates in corresponding component.

Then swap each coordinate between components if needed, by substracting and adding values.

Remember to update number of coordinates in each components

Notice, that comparing to mean step is still O(n). The swap is slower; O(log n) compared to O(1). Mean calculation is faster; O(Mlog N), where M is number of components, compared to O(N).

### Flow calculations, where each components has max 8 neighbours

Create a 2D grid, where one keep track of input flow (negative value) and output flow (positive value) in following way:

Out 0 Out 0 Out

0 In In In 0

Out In 0 In Out

0 In In In 0

Out 0 Out 0 Out

By placing adjacent components next to eachother, one can create a gigantic map where one keep track of flows between components.

Here on can use 2D fenwick to sum flow across a set of components, that corresponds to a path.

In some cases, in for examples pipe systems, number of components may be many thousands.

By placing all those thousand components (for example pipes) next to eachother, one can easily calculate netto flow in a very fast way, at the same time

one can update input and output flow for each component in a fast way.

In some cases, one may have to do multiple calculations and then sum total flow of all calculations - because one only can sum in one direction at a time, due to direction change.

It could also be a crowd sensing system, where one receive GPS coordinates that is associated with a square in a map.

By updating input and output based on square one leaved and square one entered, one can have a gigantic map of many thousands squares where

netto flow can be calculated in a fast way.

### Data aggregation in fog computing

Assume one have 1000 clients A1-A1000 , a fog computer B, and a server C.

By using B as a middle man, one can create a summary of statistic that is relevant to C; based on relevant actions (max,min,product, sum) and ranges.

Communication beteen A1-A1000 and B:

A sends (index, value, datatype, action (add/sub/prod/max/min)) to B.

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Update array[index] with corresponding action and value.

Communication between B and C:

B asks for a summary of statistics in format (index range, action, return data type).

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Use fenwick range operation corresponding to index range and action, and convert to desired data type.

### Keep track of locations of cars in a large map

By letting a bit position in a number correspond to a car, one can decide that 1 means that the car is here and 0 means it doesn't.

By adding and substracting a number where it is 1 in this position and 0 in the rest, one can add and remove a car from a location.

A map can be thought of as a grid, and therfore one can use 2D fenwick tree.

Because a number only have a maximum of 64 bits, one need a new fenwick tree for each chunk of 64 cars.

Each car is tagged with (fenwickTreeNr, bitPos), and each location is tagged with an index.

If a client knows its (fenwickTreeNr,bitPos) and know what location corresponds to what index, one can just update locally

and send the index instead of the GPS coordinate.

By doing this, the server does not really know where the car is - but it can search for it in a fast way by combinding binary search (adjust right side first, and then left) and range sum query. Its

also a more secure way of dealing with locations, compared to GPS coordinates.

### Fast Sub range integration, where values are time dependent

Recall simpsons formula:

\begin{align}

\int_a^b f(x)\, dx

&\approx \frac{1}{3} h\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2}\big[f(x_{2i - 2}) + 4f(x_{2i - 1}) + f(x_{2i})\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\big[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \dots + 2f(x_{n - 2}) + 4f(x_{n - 1}) + f(x_n)\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\left[f(x_0) + 4\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2} f(x_{2i - 1}) + 2\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2 - 1} f(x_{2i}) + f(x_n)\right].

\end{align}

By adding and substracting

\begin{align}f(x_{index}), 2f(x_{index})\end{align} , or

\begin{align}

4f(x_{index})

\end{align} , depending on index, to

array[index]; one can in a fast way recalculate the integral of sub ranges, when some values changes.

Notice that one can add new values by changing value of array[max index] and array[max index - 1] , and by adding new value to array[max index+1].

### Grid surface, and collions with small objects

A grid surface contains many squares or faces. By making a 2D fenwick tree, one can keep track of current preasure

each square.

By having a rule engine, that says:

Area >= 1000, must have p < 0.5. action if fail: rotation of relevant squares

Area >= 100, must have p <= 0.1, action if fail: animation played for relevant squares

Area >= 10, must have p <= 0.001 action if fail: translation of relevant suqares

One can check different ranges, in a fast way, to see if preasure constraint is OK.

If a constraint fail, an associated action can be used (f.ex a geometric transformation based on presure, and other parameters).

When first rule is checked for all possible ranges, one check next rule to see if a preasure constraint fail - if it does, a smaller area can be

affected by an predefined action.

Because a 2D fenwick tree is used, its possible to add and remove collisions to the grid. Such collisions could be bullets that hit a person in a 3D game, where a person

has surface grid (to simply one could have a rectangular surface grid). Rule engines controlls wether or not, one looses a finger, an arm, a head,..etc, based

on preasure distrubition). In some cases, a object may have life time - it may be removed after a fixed amount of time, or change in preasure as a function of time.

Its also handy to use 2D fenwick tree, when preasure waves is introduced (waves in water, earth quacke, explosions). Wave equations is used to predict grid squares affected, and these squares is updated accordanly. For each step (everyone is updated by a time step), one take a look on rule engine to see if some actions is triggered.
