{{Short description|Data structure}} {{Infobox data structure |name = Fenwick tree
Binary indexed tree |image = BITDemo.gif |caption = Creation of a binary indexed tree for the array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] by elementwise insertion |type = tree |invented_by = Boris Ryabko |invented_year = 1989 |space_avg = {{math|O(''n'')}} |space_worst = {{math|O(''n'')}} |search_avg = {{math|O(log''n'')}} |search_worst = {{math|O(log''n'')}} |insert_avg = {{math|O(log''n'')}} |insert_worst = {{math|O(log''n'')}} |delete_avg = {{math|O(n)}} |delete_worst = {{math|O(n)}} }} A '''Fenwick tree''' or '''binary indexed tree''' '''(BIT)''' is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate [[prefix sum]]s in a table of numbers. This structure was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989{{cite journal |author=Boris Ryabko |title=A fast on-line code |journal=Soviet Math. Dokl. |volume=39 |issue=3 |year=1989 |pages=533–537 |url=http://boris.ryabko.net/dan1989.pdf }} with a further modification published in 1992.{{cite journal |author=Boris Ryabko |title=A fast on-line adaptive code |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Theory |volume=28 |issue=1 |year=1992 |pages=1400–1404 |url=http://boris.ryabko.net/ryabko1992.pdf}} It has subsequently become known under the name Fenwick tree after [[Peter Fenwick (computer scientist)|Peter Fenwick]], who described this structure in his 1994 article.{{cite journal |author=Peter M. Fenwick |title=A new data structure for cumulative frequency tables |journal=Software: Practice and Experience |volume=24 |issue=3 |year=1994 |pages=327–336 |doi=10.1002/spe.4380240306 |citeseerx=10.1.1.14.8917 |s2cid=7519761 }} When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. A flat array of n numbers can either store the elements or the prefix sums. In the first case, computing prefix sums requires linear time; in the second case, updating the array elements requires linear time (in both cases, the other operation can be performed in constant time). Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a [[Tree (data structure)|tree]] with n+1 nodes where the value of each node in the tree is the prefix sum of the array from the index of the parent (inclusive) up to the index of the node (exclusive). The tree itself is implicit and can be stored as an array of n numbers, with the implicit root node omitted from the array. The tree structure allows the operations of element retrieval, element update, prefix sum, and range sum to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses. ==Motivation== {{main|Prefix sums#Applications}} Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the [[running total]] of values up to each index according to some [[Associative property|associative]] [[binary operation]] (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes. Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the [[arithmetic coding]] algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the [[cumulative probability]] of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case. Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero). It is also possible to construct extensions of this data structure to quickly compute cumulative sums on d-dimensional arrays in O(\log^d n) time.{{cite journal |author=Pushkar Mishra |year=2013 |title=A New Algorithm for Updating and Querying Sub-arrays of Multidimensional Arrays |arxiv=1311.6093 |doi=10.13140/RG.2.1.2394.2485 |s2cid=1561192}} ==Description== A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a [[one-based indexing|one-based array]] A[n] with n elements. The corresponding Fenwick tree has n+1 nodes with an implicit node 0 at the root. Each level k of the tree contains nodes with indices corresponding to sums of k distinct powers of 2 (with k=0 representing an empty sum 0). For example, level k=1 contains nodes 1=2^0, 2=2^1, 4=2^2, ... and level k=2 contains nodes 3=2^1 + 2^0, 5 = 2^2 + 2^0, 6 = 2^2 + 2^1, ... The parent of a given node can be found by clearing the [[Find_first_set|last set bit]] (LSB) in its index, corresponding to the smallest power of 2 in its sum. For example, the parent of 6 = 1102 is 4 = 1002 . The below diagram shows the structure of a 16-node Fenwick tree, corresponding to a 15-element array A: [[File:16-node Fenwick tree.svg|center|thumb|438x438px|Depiction of a 16-node Fenwick tree containing range sums of a 15-node array A]] Let A(i,j] = \{ A[k] \}_{k=i+1}^j. The value of a node at index i corresponds to the [[Range query (data structures)|range sum]] of elements in A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i], that is, the values of A starting after the parent's index up to the current node's index, inclusive. The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. Note that the indices in this range do '''not''' directly correspond to children of i: for example, the range of responsibility for node 2 is A(0,2] = \{A[1], A[2]\} but node 1 is not a child of node 2. The root node 0 contains the sum of the empty range A(0,0] = \{\} with value 0. Typically, the Fenwick tree is implemented as an [[implicit data structure]] using a flat array analogous to implementations of a [[binary heap]]. In this representation, the root node 0 is omitted and the array indices directly correspond to node indices in the tree (using 1-based indexing). The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time. === Max/min range query === By keeping track of min/max in following intervals, where index = k2^i (k is a odd number), one can find max/min in [l,r] range : {{cite web |title=Efficient Range Minimum Queries using Binary Indexed Trees|url=https://ioinformatics.org/journal/v9_2015_39_44.pdf}} BIT1[i] = [(k-1)2^i+1,k2^i] BIT2[i] = [k2^i,(k+1)2^i-1] This means: * One look at all nodes from first node in subtree to this node, to this node. * One look at all of the nodes, to the right of ones position, of this subtree one are part of - except the root node. By remembering smallest to the left and smallest to the right of a spesific index, in the same subtree, one can jump between different min/max based on index. A special case is where the node k2^i, that is part of both BIT1 and BIT2, is max/min. The normal [0,r] max/min query can be implemented in same way as sum/product. === Convert product to sum problem === A product problem can be converted to a sum problem, in follwing way: \prod_{i=1}^N x_i = e^{\sum_{i = 1}^N ln(x_i)} Because total number will become to large, one should not calculate e^val. One should just calculate val and then print e^val. Same strategy can be used for 2D or multidimensional subrange product. ==== Convert matrix product problem to matrix sum problem ==== When having a product of matrices, where all matrices commute with eachother (AB = BA) and all matrices are positive definite, then ln(AB) = ln(A) + ln(B) - otherwise, this is not true. Rotation in 2D commutes with eachother. Furthermore rotation matrices in 2D are semi definite when -\frac{\pi}{2} <= \theta <= \frac{\pi}{2}. Scale matrices in 2D are always postive definite, and commutes with other scale matrices. To convert from matrix product problem to matrix sum problem, one can exploit that. e^{A} \equiv \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{A^{n}}{n!} Where A = \sum_{i = 1}^N ln(A_i) Furthermore, one can diagonilze matrix A: {{block indent|em=1.2|text={{math|1=''e''''A'' = ''Ue''''D''''U''−1}}. }} , Unless one want to calculate e^A , just print out e^A instead of calculating e^A. For a 2x2 matrix, it should be simple to calculate e^A One can use that following holds for a 2x2 matrix: \lambda = \pm\sqrt{tr(A)-det(A)} Just enter \lambda and values from matrix A to construct U and U^{-1}. U^{-1} is easy to find, due to inverse matrix formula for 2x2 matrices. Given rotation matrix : A = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\alpha) & -\sin(\alpha) \\ \sin(\alpha) & \cos(\alpha) \\ \end{pmatrix}. It can be shown that following holds, by checking against e^{M} \equiv \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{M^{n}}{n!} : ln(A) = B_n=(\alpha+2\pi n) \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix} , for all n. For matrix on form A = \tfrac{1}{q}\begin{pmatrix}r & p \\ p & r \end{pmatrix} one also see, by checking against e^{M} \equiv \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{M^{n}}{n!} : ln(A)=\begin{pmatrix}0 & a \\ a & 0 \end{pmatrix} where a = log(p + r) − log q === Sum range query === To find the prefix sum up to any given index (the ''"range query"'' operation), add up the values of nodes along the path from the current index to the root of the tree (which is trivially an empty sum, 0). The number of values to add (excluding the implicit root) is equal to the number of 1-bits in the index, and is at most \lceil\log_2 n\rceil, giving a time complexity of O(\log n). For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1-bits, so three node values must be added: those at nodes 11=10112, 10=10102, and 8=10002 (the implicit root node of 00002 can be ignored). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,10], and A[1,8], respectively (where A[i,j] = {A[i], A[i+1], ..., A[j]}) . === Point sum update using a function f(x) === To make an sum update, one need to subtract inverse of old value before adding new value. f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 & \quad \text{if }x \text{ is even}\\ x+5 & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is odd} \end{cases} f^{-1}(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{x^2} & \quad \text{if }x \text{ is even}\\ \frac{1}{x+5} & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is odd} \end{cases} The update can be done in following way: \delta \leftarrow f(A[i]_\mathrm{new}) - f^{-1}(A[i]_\mathrm{old})) BIT[i] \leftarrow BIT[i] + \delta ==== Filter function ==== In some cases one may want to sum numbers that are even numbers, larger or smaller than a spesific number, ...etc To do that, one can use a filter function. Following function only updates even numbers, and add 0 when numbers are not even. f(x) = \begin{cases} x & \quad \text{if }x \text{ is even}\\ 0 & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is odd} \end{cases} === product point update === In sum update, what one did was subtracting inverse of previous number followed by adding a new number. One didnt have to think about this, because both inverse and new number was added at same time - by adding the difference. Because product has associative, commulative and inverse property, one can do the same thing here. One divide by previous number, and multiply new number. That is: \delta = \frac{A[i]_\mathrm{new}}{A[i]_\mathrm{old}} and BIT[i] \leftarrow BIT[i] * \delta === Sum point update === To update the value in a Fenwick tree at index i (corresponding to assigning A[i] a new value) (the ''"point update"'' operation): * Compute the delta \delta = A[i]_\mathrm{new} - A[i]_\mathrm{old}. * Then, while index i \leq n: ** Update the index by adding LSB: i \leftarrow i + (i\ \&\ (-i)) ** Add \delta to the value at node i. When doing sum, one go to the left (downwards) - where one did not add values in add(index,delta), except for index one are standing on. In add(index,delta), one added to the parents from this index - that is to the right. Because of this, one dont risk adding same value delta twice. Intuitively, this can be thought of as updating each node (starting with i and iterating in increasing order) whose range of responsibility includes A[i]. For example, updating value 11=10112 in a 16-element array requires updating 10112, (10112 + 12 = 11002), and (11002 + 1002 = 100002). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,12], and A[1,16], respectively. Again, the maximum number of nodes that need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array, \lceil\log_2 n\rceil, and the time complexity is thus O(\log n). === Building the tree === A naive way to construct the tree would be to initialize the tree values to 0 and perform n point updates, yielding a time complexity of O(n\log n). However, an alternate approach uses [[dynamic programming]] to build the tree up incrementally along increasing indices. Initialization proceeds as follows: * Copy array A[n] into array T[n] containing tree values * For each index ''i'' from 1 to n: ** Let j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)). This is the first node larger than i that contains A[i] in its range of responsibility. ** If j \leq n, update value of node at j: T[j] \leftarrow T[j] + T[i] It can be shown that at the point that index i is reached in the loop, T[i] is already the correct Fenwick value for node i. If i is a leaf node (with only one element in its range of responsibility) this holds trivially. If i is an internal node, the loop ensures that it has been updated with all range sums within its own range, so it will contain the correct Fenwick value. For example, at step i=4, node 4 (with initial value A[4]) will have been incremented by T[2] (which contains the sum A[1] + A[2]) and T[3] (which contains the value A[3]), and thus will contain the range sum A(0,4] of the first 4 elements of the tree. Since each update happens at most once per index, the resulting algorithm is O(n) time complexity. This can also be done in-place in the original array, eliminating the copy and additional storage for T[n]. An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n], by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep. A less efficient O(n) algorithm for constructing the tree works in two passes: first convert A[n] to a prefix sum (which takes O(n) time), then iterating backwards from n..1, compute each node's range sum by computing the difference of prefix sums: \Sigma A(\mathrm{parent}(i), i] = \Sigma A(0, i] - \Sigma A(0, \mathrm{parent}(i)].{{Cite web |title=Fenwick tree: initialization in O(N) |url=https://codeforces.com/blog/entry/59305 |access-date=2023-01-23 |website=Codeforces |language=en}} === Extension to multiple dimensions === A ''2D Fenwick tree (2D BIT)'' can be constructed as a 1D Fenwick tree where each node of the tree contains a 1D Fenwick tree, and stores range sums for submatrices of a 2D matrix ''A''[m,n]. The tree representation remains implicit and the data is stored in an ''m'' x ''n'' array where position (i, j) in the array corresponds to the jth node of the ith Fenwick tree. Point update and range query are implemented similarly to the 1D case, but using nested loops (iterating along the column dimension (sub-tree) in the inner loop, and iterating along the row dimension (main tree) in the outer loop). This idea can be extended to tensors with arbitrary number of dimensions ''d,'' with time complexity O(\log^d n) for range-query and point-update (assuming the tensor is size ''n'' along each axis). === Fenwick tree as a compression of a binary tree === A binary tree can be compressed to a fenwick tree, if and only if, for every even leaf node in binary tree (indexed 2n, n is integer ), it is has the same property as its parents, up to the point; the smallest sub-tree that is possible to make,connecting as many nodes as possible, is created To decompress, just do the opposit as done in compression Subtrees may also be compressed to fenwick tree. Furthermore, if only small changes is needed to make an fenwick compression, one should remember and do necessery changes - with the changes as extra information, to enable decompression. ==== Generate fenwick compressable binary tree from its leafs ==== A fenwick compressable binary tree can be generated from its leaf nodes, if all leaf nodes with index k2^i is connected to node with index 2^i(k+1) in such a way node with index 2^i(k+1) is parent of node with index k2^i. To find 2^i term in val = k2^i, use val & (-val). Parent node is then: (val & (-val)) + k2^i Example: Node 14 is connected to node 16, because 14 = 7*2 and 16 = 7*2 +2. 4 is connected to 8, because 4 = 2^2 and 8 = 2^2 + 2^2 12 is connected to 16 because, 12 = 3*(2^2) and 16 = 3*(2^2) + 2^2 ==== Finding i and k ==== Recall 2^i = (val & (-val)), where val = k2^i. By simple algebraic manipulation, one see that: k = val / (val & (-val)) By using ln, and some simple algebraic manipulation, one see that: i = ln (val / k) / ln(2), where val = k2^i. ===== Multiple nodes that has same parent ===== How to handle cases where a several nodes have this node as parent? Because first parent can have 1 child, second parent can have 2 childs, third parent can have 3 childs,counted from index 1 .One place a node in a index, such that there are enough childs. If one have to many childs, one can make them dummy nodes - that just takes up space. A parent childs, counted from index 1 with N childs, have childs that can have N-1,N-2,...2,1,0 (or N-1,N-2,...2,1 if it is a root node) childs where closest child only can have 1 or 0 childs, depending on whether it is a root node or not. Furthermore; longest sequence length from leaf node to this node, is equal to number of possible childs for this node. As a consequence; it is only possible to add a tree to a node in fenwick tree, if: * If longest sequence is length N, the node that adds the tree must have the possibility to add at least N childs. * For each node in subtree, all direct childs of same node must have a unique number of childs. That is; no two direct childs of same node, can have same number of childs. * Every sequence from node in subtree to leaf, must have a strictly descending sequence of number of childs ===== Node that has no parent ===== To handle the case where a node has no parent, one can make itself a dummy node. Such a node can reset the value to 0 or 1, when going to parent doing prefix sum and prefix product - it kinda forget the sum and product so far. ==Implementation== === Basic implementation in [[C (programming language)|C]] === // SIZE should be 1 + a power of 2. int A[SIZE]; // Least Significant Bit of i having a value of 1 #define LSB(i) ((i) & -(i)) // Returns the sum of the first i elements (indices 0 to i) // Equivalent to range_sum(0, i) int prefix_sum(int i) { int sum = A[0]; for (; i != 0; i -= LSB(i)) sum += A[i]; return sum; } // Add delta to element with index i (zero-based) void add(int i, int delta) { if (i == 0) { A[0] += delta; return; } for (; i < SIZE; i+= LSB(i)) A[i] += delta; } === Useful functions in [[C (programming language)|C]] === // Returns the sum of elements from i + 1 to j // Equivalent to prefix_sum(j) - prefix_sum(i), but slightly faster int range_sum(int i, int j) { int sum = 0; for (; j > i; j -= LSB(j)) sum += A[j]; for (; i > j; i -= LSB(i)) sum -= A[i]; return sum; } // Convert A[] in place to Fenwick tree form void init(void) { for (int i = 1; i < SIZE; ++i) { int j = i + LSB(i); if (j < SIZE) A[j] += A[i]; } } // Convert back to array of per-element counts void fini(void) { for (int i = SIZE - 1; i > 0; --i) { int j = i + LSB(i); if (j < SIZE) A[j] -= A[i]; } } // Return a single element's value int get(int i) { return range_sum(i, i + 1); } // Set (as opposed to adjust) a single element's value void set(int i, int value) { add(i, value - get(i)); } // Find the largest i with prefix_sum(i) <= value. // NOTE: Requires that all values are non-negative! unsigned int rank_query(int value) { int i = 0, j = SIZE - 1; // j is a power of 2. value -= A[0]; for (; j > 0; j >>= 1) { if (i + j < SIZE && A[i + j] <= value) { value -= A[i + j]; i += j; } } return i; } === Implementation in [[C++]] === class FenwickTree { private: vector data; int getParent(int i) const { return i - (i & (-i)); } int getNext(int i) const { return i + (i & (-i)); } public: FenwickTree(int n) : data(n+1, 0) { } int getSum(int i) const { int sum = 0; ++i; while (i > 0) { sum += data[i]; i = getParent(i); } return sum; } void update(int i, int v) { ++i; while (i < data.size()) { data[i] += v; i = getNext(i); } } }; ==Applications== ===Keeping track of positions problem=== Assume one have a set of elements, with an integer displacement. Then Array[i] would store relative displacement to previous element, where i is an element number. By taking range sum between i and j, one would get the relative distance between object i and j. A concrete real example of this would be tags in html file, where one keep track of line numbers of every element when an element is moved. To get a position, one simply take the range sum between two elements. === Finding angle that makes a ray hit maximum number of mirrors, using bounding primitives === Let fenwick tree be a tree representing number of mirrors that is hit by incoming angles, for a ray from a spesific point, against 2D bounding primives (circle and squares) surounding smaller bounding primitves, a group of mirrors or a mirror. A mirror can have different ranges for incoming rays on left side, and incoming rays on right side. If one use k-means multiple times, one can create a tree. Who is parent and who is child must be placed into fenwick tree.This is done such that an update of accepted incoming range, of a mirror, gets updated to its bouding primitvie, and further upward in the tree - bounding primitives sums accepted ranges for a mirror to other accepted ranges for mirrors. By using range search, one can find angles of ray, from a spesific point, that hits maximum number of mirrors - that in some cases could be all mirrors. === Sub-range product of transformation matrices=== Create two fenwick trees, one with product over inverses and one with product of its usal matrices. To find sub-range product, take product range of matrices in inverse fenwick tree to left side of range. Remember this matrix. Now, take product range of matrices in fenwick tree to right side of range. Take product of this matrix with the inverse matrix one got from inverse fenwick tree. One cannot update matrix in a easy way though, due to lack of commulativity in matrix product. ==== Transforming product problem to sum problem ==== When having product of matrices, where all matrices commute with eachother (AB = BA) and all matrices are positive definite, then ln(AB) = ln(A) + ln(B) - otherwise, this is not true. Rotation in 2D commutes with eachother. Furthermore rotation matrices in 2D are semi definite when -\frac{\pi}{2} <= \theta <= \frac{\pi}{2}. Scale matrices in 2D are always postive definite, and commutes with other scale matrices. If one have such matrices, commutative and positive definite, one can do the following: \prod_{i=1}^N A_i = e^{\sum_{i = 1}^N ln(A_i)} Instead of focusing on products of matrices,find: \sum_{i = 1}^N ln(A_i) and then calculate: \prod_{i=1}^N A_i = e^{\sum_{i = 1}^N ln(A_i)} Because of the nature of 2x2 matrices, e^A can easily be transformed to a matrix B. In case one have sub ranges that comutes, but not to all matrices outside sub range, one may go for the sub-ranges and do the following: \prod_{i=1}^N A_i = e^{\sum_{i = 1}^a ln(A_i)}e^{\sum_{i = a+1}^b ln(A_i)}e^{\sum_{i = b+1}^c ln(A_i)}e^{\sum_{i = c+1}^N ln(A_i)} = e^{M}e^{N}e^{O}e^{P} === Longest increasing subsequence === Consider a sequence 8 5 7 3 1 2 9 4 6 For each element v added, update A[i] s.t: A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1, such that array[x] <= array[i]. array[x] <= array[i] can be ensured, by letting i= array[index in list]. This leaves ous with: A[i] = max(0 <= x < i) A[x] + 1, A running example: #A[array[0]] = A[8] = max (0 <= x < 8) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1 #A[array[1]] = A[5] = max (0 <= x < 5) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0,0,...,0) + 1 = 1 #A[array[2]] = A[7] = max (0 <= x < 7) A[x]+ 1 = max(A[0],[1],A[2],A[3],A[4],A[5],A[6]) + 1 = A[5] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2 #A[array[3]] = A[3] = max (0 <= x < 3) A[x] + 1 = max(0,0,0...,0) + 1 = 1 #A[array[4]] = A[1] = max (0 <= x < 1) A[x] + 1 = max(A[0]) + 1 = 1 #A[array[5]] = A[2] = max (0 <= x < 2) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1) + 1 = 2 #A[array[6]] = A[9] = max (0 <= x < 9) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,0,1,0,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3 #A[array[7]] = A[4] = max (0 <= x < 4) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1) + 1 = 2+1 = 3 #A[array[8]] = A[6] = max (0 <= x < 6) A[x] + 1 = max(0,1,2,1,3,1) + 1 = 3+1 = 4 That corresponds well to the answer 1,2,4,6 If max element is to large, one can use number compression by using sorting That is i= indexInSortedList[index in not sorted list], instead of i = array[index in not sorted list] Take this example: * Array: 166,32,44,66,88 * Sorted: 32,44,66,88,166 Then: A[indexInSortedList[0]] = A[4], and we are back to the problem we are used to === Moment of intertia calculation === By using 4 fenwick trees; one for mass at point , one for distance to x-axis , one for distance to y-axis, and last one for distance to z-axis, for each element (x,y,z) in set associated with a object in 3D-space; one can use following formula to keep track of moment of intertia, due to deformation (change of x,y,z for some points) or mass loss (change of mass at some points): \mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix} I_{xx} & I_{xy} & I_{xz} \\ I_{yx} & I_{yy} & I_{yz} \\ I_{zx} & I_{zy} & I_{zz} \end{bmatrix} where \begin{align} I_{xx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(y_{k}^{2} + z_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(y_{k}) + ln(z_{k}))} } \\ I_{yy} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(x_{k}^{2} + z_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(x_{k}) + ln(z_{k}))} } \\ I_{zz} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(x_{k}^{2} + y_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(x_{k}) + ln(y_{k}))} } \end{align} \begin{align} I_{xy} = I_{yx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} x_{k} y_{k} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(x_{k})+ln( y_{k})} \\ I_{xz} = I_{zx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} x_{k} z_{k} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(x_{k})+ln( z_{k})} \\ I_{yz} = I_{zy} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} y_{k} z_{k} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(y_{k})+ln( z_{k})} \end{align} All vertices should be mapped to a unique index, associated with fenwick tree - the index will be same for all 4 fenwick trees. They should be sorted by x,y,z - first by x, second by y and last by z; if one want to focus on deformation for an fixed (y,z). By sorting diffrentily, one can get a fixed (x,y) or (x,z) with sorted coordinates along an axis. === Find range with smallest sum that contains all elements in set S === Main idea: Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S. One has a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurrence is remembered, removing elements from left side won't do any damage. One can check if an element is already found, by checking it against an array of indexes of last occurrence for this number. Furthermore, one can check if index one is standing on, is last occurrence by comparing with index in array. for all elements in array: if array[i] is not in S: #Element is new elif A[array[i]] is 0: A[array[i]] = i elementFound = elementFound + 1 else: #update index of last occurance of this number A[array[i]] = i if elementsFound = nmb elements in S: rangeSum = calculate range sum for range if rangeSum < smallestRangeSum: smallestRangeSum = rangeSum bestLeftIdx = left index bestRightIdx = i if A[array[left index]] = left index: elementsFound = elementFound - 1 A[array[left index]] = 0 left index = left index +1 while A[array[left index]] not left index or array[left index] not in S: left index = left index + 1 i=i+1 If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting. That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]] By using same approach, one can find range with smallest sum that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S. === Fast mean square error calculation === From mean square error formula, one can observe that: \begin{align} &\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\big(x_i-\bar{x}\big)^2 =\frac{1}{n}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n}x_i^2 - 2\bar{x}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}x_i + \bar{x}^2)\\ \end{align} This means that if one have two fenwick trees; one for x_i and one for x_i^2 , one can in a fast way update both of these terms in a fast way. Average \bar{x} can be found through range sum query, where one divide answer with number of elements. One find the sum of x_i , and average \bar{x} at same time. After finding x_i , one can just multiply it with -2\bar{x} get last term. Sum of x_i^2 is found by range summing the same elements, in the other fenwick tree. Add all terms together, and divide with number of elements to get final answer. By doing this one can update in O(log N) and calculate sub-ranges in O(log N) === Find smallest range that contains all elements in set S === Main idea: Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S. One have a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurence is remembered, removing elements from left side wont do any damage. By setting values of last occurence of element in set S to 1, value not in set S to 0, and elment in S that is not last occurence to 0, one can use fenwick tree combined with range sum to find smallest range that contains all elements in set S. for all elements in array: if array[i] is not in S: update(fenw[i],0) elif A[array[i]] is not 0: #Make sure to remove previous occurence of array[i] from range sum, by updating value on this index to 0. #Remember index of last occurence of element array[i], that is in set S update(fenw[A[array[i]]],0) update(fenw[i],1) A[array[i]] = i else: update(fenw[i],1) A[array[i]] = i calculate range sum of 0 and 1 if sum is equal to number of elements in S: length = i - left index if length < smallest length: smallest length = length leftIndexSol = left index rightIndexSol = i #Optmization, to avoid doing to many range sums. while left index isn't a last occurence of a number in set S: left index = left index + 1 i=i+1 If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting. That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]] By using same approach, one can find smallest range that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S. === Use of fenwick in k-mean algorithm, to make mean calculation faster === Create a sepreate fenwick tree for x and y coordinate. Allocate empty space for coordinates to a variable N (max number of coordinates for each component) for each M components. Each of the empty spaces has value 0. Create a list of initial means, and allocate coordinates to nearest mean (update empty allocated space, corresponding to component associated with mean, in fenwick tree). Remember to keep track of number of coordinates in each component. After this is done, find sum of each component and divide by number of coordinates in corresponding component. Then swap each coordinate between components if needed, by substracting and adding values. Remember to update number of coordinates in each components Notice, that comparing to mean step is still O(n). The swap is slower; O(log n) compared to O(1). Mean calculation is faster; O(Mlog N), where M is number of components, compared to O(N). === Flow calculations, where each components has max 8 neighbours === Create a 2D grid, where one keep track of input flow (negative value) and output flow (positive value) in following way: Out 0 Out 0 Out 0 In In In 0 Out In 0 In Out 0 In In In 0 Out 0 Out 0 Out By placing adjacent components next to eachother, one can create a gigantic map where one keep track of flows between components. Here on can use 2D fenwick to sum flow across a set of components, that corresponds to a path. In some cases, in for examples pipe systems, number of components may be many thousands. By placing all those thousand components (for example pipes) next to eachother, one can easily calculate netto flow in a very fast way, at the same time one can update input and output flow for each component in a fast way. In some cases, one may have to do multiple calculations and then sum total flow of all calculations - because one only can sum in one direction at a time, due to direction change. It could also be a crowd sensing system, where one receive GPS coordinates that is associated with a square in a map. By updating input and output based on square one leaved and square one entered, one can have a gigantic map of many thousands squares where netto flow can be calculated in a fast way. === Data aggregation in fog computing === Assume one have 1000 clients A1-A1000 , a fog computer B, and a server C. By using B as a middle man, one can create a summary of statistic that is relevant to C; based on relevant actions (max,min,product, sum) and ranges. Communication beteen A1-A1000 and B: # A sends (index, value, datatype, action (add/sub/prod/max/min)) to B. # B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2. # Update array[index] with corresponding action and value. Communication between B and C: # B asks for a summary of statistics in format (index range, action, return data type). # B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2. # Use fenwick range operation corresponding to index range and action, and convert to desired data type. === Keep track of locations of cars in a large map === By letting a bit position in a number correspond to a car, one can decide that 1 means that the car is here and 0 means it doesn't. By adding and substracting a number where it is 1 in this position and 0 in the rest, one can add and remove a car from a location. A map can be thought of as a grid, and therfore one can use 2D fenwick tree. Because a number only have a maximum of 64 bits, one need a new fenwick tree for each chunk of 64 cars. Each car is tagged with (fenwickTreeNr, bitPos), and each location is tagged with an index. If a client knows its (fenwickTreeNr,bitPos) and know what location corresponds to what index, one can just update locally and send the index instead of the GPS coordinate. By doing this, the server does not really know where the car is - but it can search for it in a fast way by combinding binary search (adjust right side first, and then left) and range sum query. Its also a more secure way of dealing with locations, compared to GPS coordinates. === Fast Sub range integration, where values are time dependent === Recall simpsons formula: \begin{align} \int_a^b f(x)\, dx &\approx \frac{1}{3} h\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2}\big[f(x_{2i - 2}) + 4f(x_{2i - 1}) + f(x_{2i})\big]\\ &= \frac{1}{3} h\big[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \dots + 2f(x_{n - 2}) + 4f(x_{n - 1}) + f(x_n)\big]\\ &= \frac{1}{3} h\left[f(x_0) + 4\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2} f(x_{2i - 1}) + 2\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2 - 1} f(x_{2i}) + f(x_n)\right]. \end{align} By adding and substracting \begin{align}f(x_{index}), 2f(x_{index})\end{align} , or \begin{align} 4f(x_{index}) \end{align} , depending on index, to array[index]; one can in a fast way recalculate the integral of sub ranges, when some values changes. Notice that one can add new values by changing value of array[max index] and array[max index - 1] , and by adding new value to array[max index+1]. === Grid surface, and collions with small objects === A grid surface contains many squares or faces. By making a 2D fenwick tree, one can keep track of current preasure each square. By having a rule engine, that says: #Area >= 1000, must have p < 0.5. action if fail: rotation of relevant squares #Area >= 100, must have p <= 0.1, action if fail: animation played for relevant squares #Area >= 10, must have p <= 0.001 action if fail: translation of relevant suqares One can check different ranges, in a fast way, to see if preasure constraint is OK. If a constraint fail, an associated action can be used (f.ex a geometric transformation based on presure, and other parameters). When first rule is checked for all possible ranges, one check next rule to see if a preasure constraint fail - if it does, a smaller area can be affected by an predefined action. Because a 2D fenwick tree is used, its possible to add and remove collisions to the grid. Such collisions could be bullets that hit a person in a 3D game, where a person has surface grid (to simply one could have a rectangular surface grid). Rule engines controlls wether or not, one looses a finger, an arm, a head,..etc, based on preasure distrubition). In some cases, a object may have life time - it may be removed after a fixed amount of time, or change in preasure as a function of time. Its also handy to use 2D fenwick tree, when preasure waves is introduced (waves in water, earth quacke, explosions). Wave equations is used to predict grid squares affected, and these squares is updated accordanly. For each step (everyone is updated by a time step), one take a look on rule engine to see if some actions is triggered. ==See also== * [[Order statistic tree]] * [[Prefix sums]] * [[Segment tree]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== * [https://www.topcoder.com/community/data-science/data-science-tutorials/binary-indexed-trees/ A tutorial on Fenwick Trees on TopCoder] * [http://www.algorithmist.com/index.php/Fenwick_tree An article on Fenwick Trees on Algorithmist] * [http://michaelnielsen.org/polymath1/index.php?title=Updating_partial_sums_with_Fenwick_tree An entry on Fenwick Trees on Polymath wiki] *[https://cs.stackexchange.com/q/10538 stack exchange] {{CS-Trees}} [[Category:Trees (data structures)]] [[Category:Soviet inventions]] [[Category:Russian inventions]]

A Fenwick tree or binary indexed tree (BIT) is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers.

This structure was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989[1]

with a further modification published in 1992.[2]

It has subsequently become known under the name Fenwick tree after Peter Fenwick, who described this structure in his 1994 article.[3]

When compared with a flat array of numbers, the Fenwick tree achieves a much better balance between two operations: element update and prefix sum calculation. A flat array of n numbers can either store the elements or the prefix sums. In the first case, computing prefix sums requires linear time; in the second case, updating the array elements requires linear time (in both cases, the other operation can be performed in constant time). Fenwick trees allow both operations to be performed in O(\log n) time. This is achieved by representing the numbers as a tree with n+1 nodes where the value of each node in the tree is the prefix sum of the array from the index of the parent (inclusive) up to the index of the node (exclusive). The tree itself is implicit and can be stored as an array of n numbers, with the implicit root node omitted from the array. The tree structure allows the operations of element retrieval, element update, prefix sum, and range sum to be performed using only O(\log n) node accesses.

## Motivation

Given a table of elements, it is sometimes desirable to calculate the running total of values up to each index according to some associative binary operation (addition on integers being by far the most common). Fenwick trees provide a method to query the running total at any index, in addition to allowing changes to the underlying value table and having all further queries reflect those changes.

Fenwick trees are particularly designed to implement the arithmetic coding algorithm, which maintains counts of each symbol produced and needs to convert those to the cumulative probability of a symbol less than a given symbol. Development of operations it supports were primarily motivated by use in that case.

Using a Fenwick tree it requires only O(\log n) operations to compute any desired cumulative sum, or more generally the sum of any range of values (not necessarily starting at zero). It is also possible to construct extensions of this data structure to quickly compute cumulative sums on d -dimensional arrays in O(\log^d n) time.[4]

## Description

A Fenwick tree is most easily understood by considering a one-based array A[n] with n elements. The corresponding Fenwick tree has n+1 nodes with an implicit node 0 at the root. Each level k of the tree contains nodes with indices corresponding to sums of k distinct powers of 2 (with k=0 representing an empty sum 0). For example, level k=1 contains nodes 1=2^0, 2=2^1, 4=2^2, ... and level k=2 contains nodes 3=2^1 + 2^0, 5 = 2^2 + 2^0, 6 = 2^2 + 2^1, ... The parent of a given node can be found by clearing the last set bit (LSB) in its index, corresponding to the smallest power of 2 in its sum. For example, the parent of 6 = 1102 is 4 = 1002 .

The below diagram shows the structure of a 16-node Fenwick tree, corresponding to a 15-element array A:

Let A(i,j] = \{ A[k] \}_{k=i+1}^j . The value of a node at index i corresponds to the range sum of elements in A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] , that is, the values of A starting after the parent's index up to the current node's index, inclusive. The elements A(\mathrm{parent}(i),i] are considered to be the "range of responsibility" for the current node[3] and consist of \mathrm{lsb}(i) = (i\ \&\ (-i)) (where & denotes bitwise AND) elements. Note that the indices in this range do not directly correspond to children of i : for example, the range of responsibility for node 2 is A(0,2] = \{A[1], A[2]\} but node 1 is not a child of node 2. The root node 0 contains the sum of the empty range A(0,0] = \{\} with value 0.

Typically, the Fenwick tree is implemented as an implicit data structure using a flat array analogous to implementations of a binary heap. In this representation, the root node 0 is omitted and the array indices directly correspond to node indices in the tree (using 1-based indexing).

The initial process of building the Fenwick tree over a table of values runs in O(n log n) time. Other efficient operations include locating the index of a value if all values are positive, or all indices with a given value if all values are non-negative. Also supported is the scaling of all values by a constant factor in O(n) time.

### Max/min range query

By keeping track of min/max in following intervals, where index = k2^i (k is a odd number), one can find max/min in [l,r] range :

[5]

BIT1[i] = [(k-1)2^i+1,k2^i]

BIT2[i] = [k2^i,(k+1)2^i-1]

This means:

One look at all nodes from first node in subtree to this node, to this node.

One look at all of the nodes, to the right of ones position, of this subtree one are part of - except the root node.

By remembering smallest to the left and smallest to the right of a spesific index, in the same subtree, one can jump between different min/max based on index.

A special case is where the node k2^i, that is part of both BIT1 and BIT2, is max/min.

The normal [0,r] max/min query can be implemented in same way as sum/product.

### Counting occurences of max/min

When looking for one occurence, one dont care if its in BIT1, BIT2, or is a root node of a sub tree.

If one are to find all occurences, one need to count all occurences in BIT1, BIT2 and the root node.

Root node could have competed against a number that is equal, and same thing goes for nodes in BIT1 and BIT2.

Both BIT1,BIT2 and root node may contain occurence of max/min.

By remembering occurence of max/min at each node, that is update occurence by 1 if value is equal, one can keep track of occurences of min/max. If added or changed value is larger, one must replace occurence with 1.

Because BIT2 always is to the right, and because BIT1 always is to the left, one can easily find the leftmost and rightmost occurence of max/min in range [l,r]

One could also find the k'th occurence of max/min in range, by looking at occurences to get an idea where the k'th occurence may be in [l,r].

### Sum range query

To find the prefix sum up to any given index (the "range query" operation), add up the values of nodes along the path from the current index to the root of the tree (which is trivially an empty sum, 0). The number of values to add (excluding the implicit root) is equal to the number of 1-bits in the index, and is at most \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , giving a time complexity of O(\log n) .

For example, say one wishes to find the sum of the first eleven values. Eleven is 10112 in binary. This contains three 1-bits, so three node values must be added: those at nodes 11=10112, 10=10102, and 8=10002 (the implicit root node of 00002 can be ignored). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,10], and A[1,8], respectively (where A[i,j] = {A[i], A[i+1], ..., A[j]}) .

### Use of multiple fenwick trees

Because fenwick tree is just an array, with clever jumping between mechanism, one can have 100-500 of those. This is handy, when each fenwick tree does not contain more than 100 000 elements. It may also be possible to have 10 000 fenwick trees, if there is no more than 1000 elements in each.

This may be needed in cases where a node have multiple parents. Whats important is to know what is the indexes for a node in the different fenwick trees - order of nodes may be different. Examples could be bus routes, where a node have different index in different bus routes. Another example would be a road map, where a node is a city with multiple roads connecting to it. The stored value could be a cost or a distance to next element in array (not the parent). Whats important, is that it may have different cost or distances in different fenwick trees. This means one may have to sum different [l,r] in different fenwick trees together. An example would be to find out how much time it takes from stop 450 to 90009 in a spesific bus route, and time it takes from stop 5800 to 85090 in a different one.

Use of multiple fenwick trees, reduce the multiple parents problems to multiple fenwick trees.

In some cases, one may to find range sum that crosses different fenwick trees, between start and end node. This could be thought of A[treeA][treeB][i][j] = sum[treeA][startTreeA][i] + sum[treeB][j][endTreeB], where one go from index i in tree A to index j in tree B.

This node would in this case be thought of as a root node, with one subtree in one fenwick tree and one subtree in onother.

If one have a lookup table for start and end, like startTreeA = lookup[treeA][start] and endTreeB = lookup[treeB][end], one can try all combinations to find largest or smallest sum between start and end in a set of two fenwick trees. One can use this idea further with two switching nodes, that is switching between fenwick trees two times.

To save storage, and make summation faster, one may try to only store relevant nodes in a fenwick tree. For example, if one are splitting a graph , one may add a sequence to one fenwick tree, and another to a different fenwick tree. One could think of it as; splitting a graph into different segments, where multiple nodes may have an edge to a different (or same) node in another segement.

### Point sum update using a function f(x)

To make an sum update; one need to subtract inverse of old value, before adding new value.

f(x) =

\begin{cases}

x^2 & \quad \text{if }x \text{ is even}\\

x+5 & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is odd}

\end{cases}

f^{-1}(x) =

\begin{cases}

\frac{1}{x^2} & \quad \text{if }x \text{ is even}\\

\frac{1}{x+5} & \quad \text{if } x \text{ is odd}

\end{cases}

The update can be done in following way:

\delta \leftarrow f(A[i]_\mathrm{new}) - f^{-1}(A[i]_\mathrm{old}))

BIT[i] \leftarrow BIT[i] + \delta

To do that, one can use a filter function.

Following function only updates even numbers, and add 0 when numbers are not even.

\begin{cases}

### product point update

In sum update, what one did was subtracting inverse of previous number followed by adding a new number. One didnt have to think about this, because both inverse and new number was added at same time - by adding the difference.

Because product has associative, commulative and inverse property, one can do the same thing here.

One divide by previous number, and multiply new number.

That is:

\delta = \frac{A[i]_\mathrm{new}}{A[i]_\mathrm{old}}

and

BIT[i] \leftarrow BIT[i] * \delta

### Sum point update

To update the value in a Fenwick tree at index i (corresponding to assigning A[i] a new value) (the "point update" operation):

Compute the delta \delta = A[i]_\mathrm{new} - A[i]_\mathrm{old} .

Then, while index i \leq n :

Update the index by adding LSB: i \leftarrow i + (i\ \&\ (-i))

Add \delta to the value at node i .

When doing sum, one go to the left (downwards) - where one did not add values in add(index,delta), except for index one are standing on. In add(index,delta), one added to the parents from this index - that is to the right.

Because of this, one dont risk adding same value delta twice.

Intuitively, this can be thought of as updating each node (starting with i and iterating in increasing order) whose range of responsibility includes A[i] .

For example, updating value 11=10112 in a 16-element array requires updating 10112, (10112 + 12 = 11002), and (11002 + 1002 = 100002). These contain the sums of A[11], A[9,12], and A[1,16], respectively. Again, the maximum number of nodes that need to be updated is limited by the number of bits in the size of the array, \lceil\log_2 n\rceil , and the time complexity is thus O(\log n) .

### Building the tree

A naive way to construct the tree would be to initialize the tree values to 0 and perform n point updates, yielding a time complexity of O(n\log n) . However, an alternate approach uses dynamic programming to build the tree up incrementally along increasing indices. Initialization proceeds as follows:

Copy array A[n] into array T[n] containing tree values

For each index i from 1 to n:

Let j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) . This is the first node larger than i that contains A[i] in its range of responsibility.

If j \leq n , update value of node at j: T[j] \leftarrow T[j] + T[i]

It can be shown that at the point that index i is reached in the loop, T[i] is already the correct Fenwick value for node i . If i is a leaf node (with only one element in its range of responsibility) this holds trivially. If i is an internal node, the loop ensures that it has been updated with all range sums within its own range, so it will contain the correct Fenwick value. For example, at step i=4 , node 4 (with initial value A[4] ) will have been incremented by T[2] (which contains the sum A[1] + A[2] ) and T[3] (which contains the value A[3] ), and thus will contain the range sum A(0,4] of the first 4 elements of the tree.

Since each update happens at most once per index, the resulting algorithm is O(n) time complexity. This can also be done in-place in the original array, eliminating the copy and additional storage for T[n] .

An analogous operation can be performed to convert a Fenwick tree back into the original frequency array A[n] , by iterating backwards from n to 1 and subtracting the value of j = i + (i\ \& \ (-i)) from the value of i at each timestep.

A less efficient O(n) algorithm for constructing the tree works in two passes: first convert A[n] to a prefix sum (which takes O(n) time), then iterating backwards from n..1, compute each node's range sum by computing the difference of prefix sums: \Sigma A(\mathrm{parent}(i), i] = \Sigma A(0, i] - \Sigma A(0, \mathrm{parent}(i)] .[6]

### Extension to multiple dimensions

A 2D Fenwick tree (2D BIT) can be constructed as a 1D Fenwick tree where each node of the tree contains a 1D Fenwick tree,[4] and stores range sums for submatrices of a 2D matrix A[m,n]. The tree representation remains implicit and the data is stored in an m x n array where position (i, j) in the array corresponds to the jth node of the ith Fenwick tree.

Point update and range query are implemented similarly to the 1D case, but using nested loops (iterating along the column dimension (sub-tree) in the inner loop, and iterating along the row dimension (main tree) in the outer loop).

This idea can be extended to tensors with arbitrary number of dimensions d, with time complexity O(\log^d n) for range-query and point-update (assuming the tensor is size n along each axis).

it is has the same property as its parents, up to the point; the smallest sub-tree that is possible to make,connecting as many nodes as possible, is created

To decompress, just do the opposit as done in compression

### Generate fenwick compressable binary tree from its leafs

A fenwick compressable binary tree can be generated from its leaf nodes, if all leaf nodes with index k2^i is connected to node with index 2^i(k+1)

in such a way node with index 2^i(k+1) is parent of node with index k2^i. To find 2^i term in val = k2^i, use val & (-val). Parent node is then: (val & (-val)) + k2^i

Example:

Node 14 is connected to node 16, because 14 = 7*2 and 16 = 7*2 +2.

4 is connected to 8, because 4 = 2^2 and 8 = 2^2 + 2^2

12 is connected to 16 because, 12 = 3*(2^2) and 16 = 3*(2^2) + 2^2

### Finding i and k

By simple algebraic manipulation, one see that:

k = val / (val & (-val))

By using ln, and some simple algebraic manipulation, one see that:

i = ln (val / k) / ln(2), where val = k2^i.

### Multiple nodes that has same parent

How to handle cases where a several nodes have this node as parent?

Because first parent can have 1 child, second parent can have 2 childs, third parent can have 3 childs,counted from index 1

.One place a node in a index, such that there are enough childs. If one have to many childs, one can make them dummy nodes - that just takes up space.

A parent childs, counted from index 1 with N childs, have childs that can have N-1,N-2,...2,1,0 (or N-1,N-2,...2,1 if it is a root node) childs where closest child only can have 1 or 0 childs, depending on whether it is a root node or not. Furthermore; longest sequence length from leaf node to this node, is equal to number of possible childs for this node.

As a consequence; it is only possible to add a tree to a node in fenwick tree, if:

If longest sequence is length N, the node that adds the tree must have the possibility to add at least N childs.

For each node in subtree, all direct childs of same node must have a unique number of childs. That is; no two direct childs of same node, can have same number of childs.

Every sequence from node in subtree to leaf, must have a strictly descending sequence of number of childs

### Moment of intertia calculation

By using 4 fenwick trees; one for mass at point , one for distance to x-axis , one for distance to y-axis, and last one for distance to z-axis, for each element (x,y,z) in set associated with a object in 3D-space; one can use following formula to keep track of moment of intertia, due to deformation (change of x,y,z for some points) or mass loss (change of mass at some points):

\mathbf{I} = \begin{bmatrix}

I_{xx} & I_{xy} & I_{xz} \\

I_{yx} & I_{yy} & I_{yz} \\

I_{zx} & I_{zy} & I_{zz}

\end{bmatrix}

where

\begin{align}

I_{xx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(y_{k}^{2} + z_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(y_{k}) + ln(z_{k}))} } \\

I_{yy} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(x_{k}^{2} + z_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(x_{k}) + ln(z_{k}))} } \\

I_{zz} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \sum_{k=1}^{N}{ m_{k} \left(x_{k}^{2} + y_{k}^{2}\right)} = e^{\sum_{k=1}^{N}{ ln(m_{k})+ 2(ln(x_{k}) + ln(y_{k}))} }

\end{align}

\begin{align}

I_{xy} = I_{yx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} x_{k} y_{k} = e^{-\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(x_{k})+ln( y_{k})} \\

I_{xz} = I_{zx} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} x_{k} z_{k} = e^{-\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(x_{k})+ln( z_{k})} \\

I_{yz} = I_{zy} \ &\stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ -\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} y_{k} z_{k} = e^{-\sum_{k=1}^{N} ln(m_{k})+ ln(y_{k})+ln( z_{k})}

\end{align}

All vertices should be mapped to a unique index, associated with fenwick tree - the index will be same for all 4 fenwick trees. They should be sorted by x,y,z - first by z, second by y and last by x; if one want to focus on deformation for an fixed (y,z). By sorting diferently, one can get a fixed (x,y) or (x,z) with sorted coordinates along an axis.

### Find range with smallest sum that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One has a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurrence is remembered,

removing elements from left side won't do any damage.

One can check if an element is already found, by checking it against an array of indexes of last occurrence for this number. Furthermore, one can check if index one is standing on, is last occurrence by comparing with index in array.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find range with smallest sum that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Fast mean square error calculation

From mean square error formula, one can observe that:

\begin{align}

&\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}\big(x_i-\bar{x}\big)^2 =\frac{1}{n}(\sum_{i = 1}^{n}x_i^2 - 2\bar{x}\sum_{i = 1}^{n}x_i + \bar{x}^2)\\

\end{align}

This means that if one have two fenwick trees; one for

x_i and one for x_i^2 , one can in a fast way update

both of these terms in a fast way. Average \bar{x} can be found through

range sum query, where one divide answer with number of elements. One find the sum of x_i , and average \bar{x} at same time.

After finding x_i , one can just multiply it with -2\bar{x} get last term. Sum of x_i^2 is found by range summing the same elements, in the other fenwick tree.

Add all terms together, and divide with number of elements to get final answer.

By doing this one can update in O(log N) and calculate sub-ranges in O(log N)

### Find smallest range that contains all elements in set S

Main idea:

Remember last index of each element in the sequence array, that is found in set S.

One have a range where both left and right side can be moved. Because only last occurence is remembered,

removing elements from left side wont do any damage.

By setting values of last occurence of element in set S to 1, value not in set S to 0, and elment in S that is not last occurence to 0, one

can use fenwick tree combined with range sum to find smallest range that contains all elements in set S.

If max element is to large, one can use numerical compression, by sorting.

That is A[sortedIndex[i]], instead of A[array[i]]

By using same approach, one can find smallest range that contains exactly N distinct elements from set S.

### Use of fenwick in k-mean algorithm, to make mean calculation faster

Create a sepreate fenwick tree for x and y coordinate.

Allocate empty space for coordinates to a variable N (max number of coordinates for each component) for each M components. Each of the empty spaces has value 0.

Create a list of initial means, and allocate coordinates to nearest mean (update empty allocated space, corresponding to component associated with mean, in fenwick tree).

Remember to keep track of number of coordinates in each component.

After this is done, find sum of each component and divide by number of coordinates in corresponding component.

Then swap each coordinate between components if needed, by substracting and adding values.

Remember to update number of coordinates in each components

Notice, that comparing to mean step is still O(n). The swap is slower; O(log n) compared to O(1). Mean calculation is faster; O(Mlog N), where M is number of components, compared to O(N).

### Create velocity maps, for crowd analyis

Such a fenwick appraoch is useful, when createing velocity maps, due to recalculations and lot of changes.

When analysing flow of moment, for potential sources and sinks, one can create a velocity map that changes over time as an animation. Such an animation can be analysed for patterns - common flow pattern.

To ensure privacy, x and y in (x,y) is sent seperatly at different times.

One add x and y to different fenwick trees, and do the relcalculations - with initial means equal to means found in previous calculation.

In velocity map, add position change of each mean in a 2D grid. Continue doing this, to create an animation for flow pattern analysis.

### Flow calculations, where each components has max 8 neighbours

Create a 2D grid, where one keep track of input flow (negative value) and output flow (positive value) in following way:

Out 0 Out 0 Out

0 In In In 0

Out In 0 In Out

0 In In In 0

Out 0 Out 0 Out

By placing adjacent components next to eachother, one can create a gigantic map where one keep track of flows between components.

Here on can use 2D fenwick to sum flow across a set of components, that corresponds to a path.

In some cases, in for examples pipe systems, number of components may be many thousands.

By placing all those thousand components (for example pipes) next to eachother, one can easily calculate netto flow in a very fast way, at the same time

one can update input and output flow for each component in a fast way.

In some cases, one may have to do multiple calculations and then sum total flow of all calculations - because one only can sum in one direction at a time, due to direction change.

It could also be a crowd sensing system, where one receive GPS coordinates that is associated with a square in a map.

By updating input and output based on square one leaved and square one entered, one can have a gigantic map of many thousands squares where

netto flow can be calculated in a fast way.

### Data aggregation in fog computing

Assume one have 1000 clients A1-A1000 , a fog computer B, and a server C.

By using B as a middle man, one can create a summary of statistic that is relevant to C; based on relevant actions (max,min,product, sum) and ranges.

Communication beteen A1-A1000 and B:

A sends (index, value, datatype, action (add/sub/prod/max/min)) to B.

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Update array[index] with corresponding action and value.

Communication between B and C:

B asks for a summary of statistics in format (index range, action, return data type).

B checks the action, based on add or max. If max, use fenwick tree nr 1. Else if add, use fenwick tree nr 2.

Use fenwick range operation corresponding to index range and action, and convert to desired data type.

### Keep track of locations of cars in a large map

By letting a bit position in a number correspond to a car, one can decide that 1 means that the car is here and 0 means it doesn't.

By adding and substracting a number where it is 1 in this position and 0 in the rest, one can add and remove a car from a location.

A map can be thought of as a grid, and therfore one can use 2D fenwick tree.

Because a number only have a maximum of 64 bits, one need a new fenwick tree for each chunk of 64 cars.

Each car is tagged with (fenwickTreeNr, bitPos), and each location is tagged with an index.

If a client knows its (fenwickTreeNr,bitPos) and know what location corresponds to what index, one can just update locally

and send the index instead of the GPS coordinate.

By doing this, the server does not really know where the car is - but it can search for it in a fast way by combinding binary search (adjust right side first, and then left) and range sum query. Its

also a more secure way of dealing with locations, compared to GPS coordinates.

### Fast Sub range integration, where values are time dependent

Recall simpsons formula:

\begin{align}

\int_a^b f(x)\, dx

&\approx \frac{1}{3} h\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2}\big[f(x_{2i - 2}) + 4f(x_{2i - 1}) + f(x_{2i})\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\big[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + 2f(x_4) + \dots + 2f(x_{n - 2}) + 4f(x_{n - 1}) + f(x_n)\big]\\

&= \frac{1}{3} h\left[f(x_0) + 4\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2} f(x_{2i - 1}) + 2\sum_{i = 1}^{n/2 - 1} f(x_{2i}) + f(x_n)\right].

\end{align}

By adding and substracting

\begin{align}f(x_{index}), 2f(x_{index})\end{align} , or

\begin{align}

4f(x_{index})

\end{align} , depending on index, to

array[index]; one can in a fast way recalculate the integral of sub ranges, when some values changes.

Notice that one can add new values by changing value of array[max index] and array[max index - 1] , and by adding new value to array[max index+1].

### Grid surface, and collions with small objects

A grid surface contains many squares or faces. By making a 2D fenwick tree, one can keep track of current preasure

each square.

By having a rule engine, that says:

Area >= 1000, must have p < 0.5. action if fail: rotation of relevant squares

Area >= 100, must have p <= 0.1, action if fail: animation played for relevant squares

Area >= 10, must have p <= 0.001 action if fail: translation of relevant suqares

One can check different ranges, in a fast way, to see if preasure constraint is OK.

If a constraint fail, an associated action can be used (f.ex a geometric transformation based on presure, and other parameters).

When first rule is checked for all possible ranges, one check next rule to see if a preasure constraint fail - if it does, a smaller area can be

affected by an predefined action.

Because a 2D fenwick tree is used, its possible to add and remove collisions to the grid. Such collisions could be bullets that hit a person in a 3D game, where a person

has surface grid (to simply one could have a rectangular surface grid). Rule engines controlls wether or not, one looses a finger, an arm, a head,..etc, based

on preasure distrubition). In some cases, a object may have life time - it may be removed after a fixed amount of time, or change in preasure as a function of time.

Its also handy to use 2D fenwick tree, when preasure waves is introduced (waves in water, earth quacke, explosions). Wave equations is used to predict grid squares affected, and these squares is updated accordanly. For each step (everyone is updated by a time step), one take a look on rule engine to see if some actions is triggered.
